workflows.title: Pericoronitis: local measures and antimicrobial decision
workflows.overview:
Pericoronitis is inflammation and infection of the soft tissues around a partially erupted tooth, usually a lower third molar. There is no evidence-based guidance for its clinical management, but the accepted approach mirrors any acute dental infection: local measures first, antimicrobials only as an adjunct when there is systemic spread.

## 1. Confirm the diagnosis

- Pain, swelling and tenderness around the operculum of a partially erupted tooth (most commonly the lower third molar)
- Look for trismus, halitosis, food packing under the operculum, and trauma from the opposing tooth
- Check the temperature, lymph nodes and floor of mouth before deciding on the route

## 2. Local measures (every case)

1. **Debride and irrigate** the pericoronal space with sterile solution, e.g. saline
2. **Incision and drainage** if a localised abscess is present
3. **Consider operculectomy**
4. **Occlusal adjustment** to relieve occlusion or extract the opposing tooth if it is traumatising any inflamed pericoronal tissue
5. **Analgesia**: paracetamol or ibuprofen following the NICE mild-to-moderate pain guidance
6. **Warm salty mouthwashes** at home

## 3. Decide if antimicrobials are needed

Antimicrobials are **only** added as an adjunct to local measures when there is evidence of **systemic spread**:

- **Elevated temperature**
- **Severe generalised swelling** or **cellulitis**
- **Severe localised swelling and trismus**

In the absence of these features, local measures alone are sufficient. A complex dento-facial infection arising from pericoronitis is an urgent surgical referral, not a prescription pad problem (see section 4.3 for severe spreading infections).

## 4. First-line antimicrobials

Metronidazole or amoxicillin are both effective against the obligate and facultative anaerobic bacteria that dominate pericoronitis isolates.

### Metronidazole
- **Adults**: **400 mg orally three times a day for up to 5 days**
- **Children 10-17 years**: 200-250 mg orally every 8 hours for up to 5 days

### Or amoxicillin
- **Adults**: **500 mg orally three times a day for up to 5 days**, increased if necessary to **1 g every 8 hours in severe infections**
- **Children 12-17 years**: 500 mg three times a day, increased if necessary up to 1 g three times a day in severe infections

The IV equivalents (metronidazole 500 mg 8-hourly, amoxicillin 500 mg-1 g 6 to 8-hourly) are reserved for hospital inpatients.

## 5. Once the infection is controlled

- **Recurrent episodes** (more than one) → **extract the impacted tooth** once the infection is under control, in line with NICE TA1
- Refer to oral surgery or maxillofacial surgery if extraction is not straightforward in primary care
- Review the patient at the end of the antibiotic course; failure to improve means re-checking the diagnosis, not extending the script

workflows.title: Dry socket: local management without antibiotics
workflows.overview:
Dry socket (localised osteitis or alveolar osteitis) is a recognised complication of tooth extraction. It occurs 3 to 4 days post-extraction, is self-limiting and lasts up to 10 days. Incidence is 1-4% with routine extractions but rises to 25-30% with impacted lower wisdom teeth.

The key clinical decision is straightforward: **antimicrobials are not recommended** unless there is evidence of a spreading infection.

## 1. Recognise the picture

- Severe pain starting around day 3-4 after extraction
- Empty-looking socket with loss of clot, sometimes with visible exposed bone
- Foul taste, halitosis and tender regional lymphadenitis can be present
- Temperature, severe swelling and cellulitis are **not** features of uncomplicated dry socket — if present, suspect spreading infection and reassess

## 2. Rule out a foreign body or retained root

If appropriate, take a radiograph to **exclude a foreign body or retained root** before treating as dry socket. A retained fragment will not respond to dressings.

## 3. Local measures (the entire treatment in the absence of spreading infection)

1. **Irrigate** the socket with sterile solution (e.g. saline) to remove debris
2. **Place a suitable dressing** in the socket (e.g. Alvogyl) — may relieve symptoms but can delay healing, so use judiciously
3. **Prescribe or advise analgesia** following NICE mild-to-moderate pain guidance
4. **Warm salty mouthwashes** at home
5. **Review** for resolution

## 4. Why no antibiotic

- There are no RCTs comparing antibiotics with no antibiotics in dry socket
- In the absence of signs of a spreading infection, **antimicrobials are contraindicated**
- A Cochrane review found no intervention with strong evidence of benefit; the NNT with chlorhexidine to prevent one dry socket was 232, and reported anaphylaxis cases make its preventive use controversial

## 5. When antibiotics ARE indicated (rare)

Only if signs of a **spreading infection** appear:
- Elevated temperature
- Spreading swelling or cellulitis
- Lymphadenopathy with systemic features

In that case, manage as a spreading dento-alveolar infection (see chapter 4 / abscess workflow): drainage where pus is present, plus first-line antimicrobial.

## 6. Set patient expectations

- The condition is self-limiting and lasts up to about 10 days
- Dressings give symptom relief but do not necessarily speed healing
- A second visit for redressing is often needed
- If pain worsens after 7-10 days rather than easing, return for re-assessment

workflows.title: Periodontal abscess: drainage first, antimicrobials only with systemic involvement
workflows.overview:
The periodontal abscess is a localised collection of pus in the periodontal tissues. The majority of uncomplicated periodontal swellings can be successfully managed by removing the source of infection. Antimicrobials are not the centre of treatment.

## 1. Confirm the diagnosis

- Localised swelling adjacent to a tooth with periodontal pocketing rather than periapical disease
- Pus expressible from the gingival crevice or fluctuant in soft tissue
- The tooth is usually vital; periapical radiolucency is absent or limited to the bone supporting the pocket
- Distinguish from a periapical abscess, where the tooth is non-vital and pulp testing and radiograph guide diagnosis

## 2. Definitive treatment is drainage

1. **Root surface debridement (RSD) via the pocket** — the preferred drainage route
2. **Extraction of the tooth** if the prognosis is hopeless or RSD cannot achieve drainage
3. Drain through the pocket rather than incising labially when the abscess is confined to the periodontal compartment

## 3. Decide if antimicrobials are needed

Antimicrobials are **only** indicated as an **adjunct to definitive treatment** where there is:

- **Elevated temperature**
- **Evidence of systemic spread**
- **Local lymph node involvement**

Without these features, drainage alone is the treatment.

## 4. Antimicrobial choice (when indicated)

Follow the same antimicrobial choices as for acute dento-alveolar infection (chapter 4): typically a penicillin or, for spreading anaerobic infection, metronidazole; doses and duration are those used for the acute abscess pathway.

For peri-implant disease the position is the same, only stricter:

## 5. Peri-implant disease (10.5)

- **Peri-implant mucositis**: inflammation around the implant soft tissue with no bone loss. Systemic or local antimicrobials are **not recommended**; mechanical plaque control by clinician and patient is the standard of care
- **Peri-implantitis**: inflammation with bone loss. Antimicrobials are **not recommended** as an adjunct to local management
- **Apical (retrograde) peri-implantitis**: antimicrobials alone or with surgery are **not recommended**; manage conservatively or surgically on a case-by-case basis

Where the very rare situation calls for an antimicrobial in peri-implant disease, follow the periodontitis drug choices in section 10.3.3.

## 6. Review and follow-up

- Reassess at 1-2 weeks for resolution and to plan definitive periodontal management
- Place the patient back into a periodontal care pathway: OHI, RSD where indicated, smoking cessation support, diabetes control review
- Recurrent abscesses on the same tooth flag a hopeless prognosis and the conversation moves to extraction

workflows.title: Necrotising periodontal disease: debridement plus metronidazole when systemic
workflows.overview:
Necrotising periodontal diseases are rare and include necrotising gingivitis, necrotising periodontitis and necrotising stomatitis. They are characterised by gingival necrosis and bleeding, pain and fetid breath. Severe cases may show systemic signs such as lymphadenopathy, fever and malaise.

## 1. Recognise the clinical picture

- **Necrotic interdental papillae** with characteristic punched-out, ulcerated appearance
- **Bleeding** on minimal contact
- **Pain**, often severe and disproportionate to the visible disease
- **Fetid breath** (foetor oris)
- **Pseudomembrane** (yellow-grey slough) over the necrotic tissue
- Severe cases: lymphadenopathy, raised temperature, malaise

## 2. Investigate underlying systemic factors

Necrotising periodontal disease is rare in a healthy population. Look for:

- **Smoking**
- **Stress**
- **Compromised systemic health** (HIV infection, malnutrition, immunosuppression)

Manage these in conjunction with the patient's general medical practitioner where indicated. A first presentation in an otherwise low-risk patient is an opportunity to look harder at the medical history.

## 3. Local therapy is the cornerstone

The acute phase usually resolves with local measures alone:

1. **Oral hygiene instruction** (gentle technique while painful, build up as tissues heal)
2. **Debridement under local anaesthetic** — scaling and polishing of the affected tissues
3. **Antimicrobial mouthwash** — chlorhexidine is the usual choice while brushing is too painful
4. **Adequate analgesia** following NICE mild-to-moderate pain guidance
5. **Smoking cessation support** if indicated; refer if needed

## 4. When to add antimicrobials

Antimicrobials are recommended **only as an adjunct to local measures** for necrotising periodontal disease where there is **evidence of systemic involvement**.

### Metronidazole (first choice, anaerobic flora)
- **Adults**: **400 mg orally three times a day for up to 5 days**
- **Children 10-17 years**: 200-250 mg orally every 8 hours for up to 5 days

### Amoxicillin (alternative if metronidazole contraindicated)
- **Adults**: 500 mg orally three times a day for up to 5 days, increased if necessary to 1 g every 8 hours in severe infections
- **Children 12-17 years**: 500 mg three times a day, increased if necessary up to 1 g three times a day in severe infections

Metronidazole is preferred because the infection is anaerobic. Counsel the patient on the alcohol interaction and check for warfarin co-medication before prescribing.

## 5. Review and maintenance

- Review for further treatment and maintenance once the acute phase resolves
- A limited response to treatment at review should re-open the question of underlying systemic disease (especially HIV) and prompt referral or further investigation
- Necrotising disease typically leaves crater defects in the interdental papillae; long-term periodontal maintenance is required

firstPrinciples.title: In acute dental infections antimicrobials are an adjunct to local measures, not a replacement
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: FDS-AMP repeats one structural rule across pericoronitis, dry socket, periodontal abscess and necrotising disease: drainage and removal of the cause come first; antibiotics only treat spread.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The same shape across very different infections

Pericoronitis, periodontal abscess and necrotising periodontal disease are different conditions, but the FDS-AMP recommendation in each is the same shape. Local measures resolve the condition; antimicrobials are added only where there is evidence of systemic spread [1] [2] [3].

## Why local measures lead

The pathology is a local accumulation of pus or necrotic tissue with anaerobic flora, walled off from the systemic circulation. An antibiotic does not penetrate that pus reliably; clearing the source does. The published microbiology of pericoronitis is consistent with this: most isolates are obligate and facultative anaerobic bacteria, and no single causative species is found, which is why source control matters more than empirical drug choice [4].

## What this changes for the dentist

The first decision in any acute dental infection is not which antibiotic to write but how to drain the cause. If the dentist cannot drain (no instrumentation, no time, infection too diffuse) the patient is referred, not just covered with a script. Antibiotics buy time around drainage; they do not substitute for it.

firstPrinciples.title: Pericoronitis with systemic spread is the indication for antibiotics; uncomplicated pericoronitis is local-measures only
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The same operculitis with food packing is treated very differently depending on whether the patient is febrile or not, because the threshold for antibiotics is set by systemic features.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What counts as systemic spread

The FDS-AMP threshold lists four findings that flip pericoronitis from local-measures-only to local-measures-plus-antibiotic: elevated temperature, severe generalised swelling, cellulitis, or severe localised swelling combined with trismus [1]. Without one of these, the recommendation is local treatment alone.

## What the local treatment looks like

Pericoronal debridement and irrigation, incision and drainage of any localised abscess, consideration of operculectomy, occlusal adjustment or extraction of a traumatising opposing tooth, analgesia, and warm salty mouthwashes [2]. This is a complete treatment in its own right, not a holding pattern before a script.

## Why this matters operationally

A febrile patient with severe trismus and floor-of-mouth involvement is a different problem altogether and needs urgent surgical management, not just an antibiotic [3]. Holding the line on the local-measures-only pathway in uncomplicated cases, while escalating quickly when systemic features appear, is the way the acute pericoronitis decision actually works at the chair.

firstPrinciples.title: Pericoronitis recurrence is the indication for extraction of the impacted tooth
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The relationship between NICE TA1 and FDS-AMP defines when a partially erupted third molar earns surgical removal, and recurrence of pericoronitis is the trigger that NICE accepts.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Recurrence as the threshold

FDS-AMP states that the impacted tooth should be extracted if there has been more than one episode, once infection is under control, with reference to NICE TA1 [1]. This makes a single episode of pericoronitis a watch-and-treat-locally event, but a second episode a clear referral and removal trigger.

## What "once infection is under control" means

Extracting through actively infected tissue carries higher risk of spread and worse healing. The pathway is: settle the acute episode with debridement and, if needed, antibiotics; review at the end of the course; then plan extraction [2]. The two events are not done at the same visit.

## Why the rule sits where it does

A single episode in a third molar that is still erupting may resolve with eruption itself or with a small change in the opposing occlusion. A second episode tells you that the local anatomy will keep producing the same problem, and removal of the tooth is the definitive cure. The dentist's job at the second presentation is to cover the acute infection and then refer for extraction.

firstPrinciples.title: Dry socket is self-limiting and does not need antibiotics in the absence of spreading infection
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Dry socket is painful enough that patients and clinicians often want to escalate to antibiotics, but the evidence does not support this and the FDS-AMP recommendation is explicit.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A self-limiting natural history

Dry socket occurs 3 to 4 days after extraction, is self-limiting and lasts up to 10 days [1]. The pain is significant but the condition resolves without systemic intervention.

## Why antibiotics are out

There are no RCTs comparing antibiotics with no antibiotics in dry socket. In the absence of signs of a spreading infection, antimicrobials are contraindicated, and management is centred on local measures [2]. The FDS-AMP recommendation makes this a strong recommendation despite the low quality of the evidence base, because the absence of benefit and the harms of unnecessary antibiotics fall on the same side.

## What the dentist actually does

Irrigate with saline, place a suitable dressing such as Alvogyl if symptomatic relief is needed (recognising it can delay healing), prescribe or advise analgesia, and ask for warm salty mouthwashes at home [3]. The exception that triggers antibiotics is the appearance of spreading infection: temperature, spreading swelling, lymphadenopathy. At that point the case stops being uncomplicated dry socket and is managed as a spreading dento-alveolar infection.

firstPrinciples.title: Necrotising periodontal disease is debridement plus metronidazole, with a low threshold to look for underlying systemic disease
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The drug of choice for necrotising periodontal disease comes from its anaerobic microbiology, but a poor response to treatment is the more important clinical signal.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why metronidazole, when antimicrobials are needed

The microbiology of necrotising lesions is dominated by spirochetes, fusiforms and bacteroides, all anaerobes [1]. Metronidazole is therefore the antimicrobial of choice when systemic involvement justifies a prescription, with amoxicillin used only when metronidazole is contraindicated [2].

## Local debridement does most of the work

A literature review showed that local therapeutic measures (scaling and polishing, OHI) with adequate pain control provide resolution of the acute phase of necrotising gingivitis [3]. The drug, when given, is layered on top of debridement, not used instead of it.

## What a poor response actually means

Necrotising disease in a previously healthy patient is rare. A limited response to standard treatment should re-open the medical history rather than escalate the antibiotic, especially looking for HIV, malnutrition, immunosuppression and severe smoking and stress burden. FDS-AMP advises consideration of systemic issues, especially in the presence of a limited response to treatment at review [4].

firstPrinciples.title: Periodontal abscesses are drained through the pocket; antibiotics only when systemic features appear
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Most periodontal swellings of clear periodontal origin can be cured by source control alone, which is why FDS-AMP keeps antibiotics out of the routine pathway.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The drainage route matters

The majority of uncomplicated periodontal swellings can be successfully treated by removing the source of infection. This is achieved by drainage of the abscess, ideally by RSD via the pocket, or by extraction of the tooth where prognosis is hopeless [1]. Through-the-pocket drainage uses the existing anatomy of the pocket as the path of least resistance, rather than incising labial mucosa.

## The threshold for adding antibiotics is high

FDS-AMP restricts adjunctive antibiotics to abscesses with elevated temperature, evidence of systemic spread and local lymph node involvement [2]. A localised periodontal abscess with no systemic features and a periodontium that responds to RSD does not earn a script.

## Beyond the acute episode

The abscess is a window into a wider periodontal problem. Once drained, the patient belongs back in a periodontal pathway: oral hygiene instruction, full RSD as indicated, smoking cessation, diabetes review. Recurrent abscesses on the same tooth tip the prognostic balance toward extraction and a planned restorative outcome.

firstPrinciples.title: Peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis are treated mechanically; antimicrobials are not recommended
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Implants attract the same bacterial biofilm as teeth, but the evidence base does not support adding antibiotics to mechanical therapy in either peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Mucositis: plaque control is the standard of care

Peri-implant mucositis is inflammation of the peri-implant soft tissue without bone loss, and untreated it can progress to peri-implantitis. Two RCTs and a systematic review showed that professionally and patient-administered mechanical plaque control alone reduces bleeding on probing and is the standard of care [1]. Adjunctive antimicrobials add nothing.

## Peri-implantitis: bone loss does not change the answer

With bone loss, surgical management enters the conversation, but adjunctive antimicrobials still do not. A Cochrane review of nine RCTs found no benefit from a range of antimicrobial regimens, and adjunctive antimicrobials are not recommended in the management of peri-implantitis [2].

## What this means for the GDP

A bleeding peri-implant pocket gets oral hygiene instruction, prosthesis adjustment to allow access, and mechanical debridement. Bone loss escalates to surgical assessment, not to a script. The very rare case where a peri-implant infection demands an antimicrobial follows the periodontitis drug choices in section 10.3.3 rather than a separate peri-implant regimen [3].

firstPrinciples.title: Pericoronitis microbiology is non-specific, which is why drug choice is empirical and short
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Two systematic reviews found no evidence to recommend one antimicrobial over another in odontogenic infections, which leaves drug choice driven by anaerobic cover and stewardship rather than targeted therapy.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What microbiology actually shows

Two microbiological studies of pericoronitis infections found that no causative species could be identified, but most isolates were obligate and facultative anaerobic bacteria [1]. There is no single pathogen to target.

## Why metronidazole and amoxicillin both fit

With no pathogen-specific therapy and a dominantly anaerobic flora, both metronidazole and amoxicillin are recognised as suitable choices because they both cover anaerobes [2]. The choice between them is not microbiological; it is patient-specific (interactions, allergy, compliance).

## Stewardship implications

Because two systematic reviews found no evidence to recommend one antimicrobial over another in the management of odontogenic infections [3], escalation to broader-spectrum or longer courses delivers no benefit and increases the harms of resistance and side effects. The 5-day duration cap is part of the same stewardship logic; the body fights the infection, the antibiotic protects the systemic compartment.

subjects.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis (non-cardiac)
subjects.description: FDS-AMP guidance on antibiotic prophylaxis for non-cardiac medical conditions: joint replacements, prosthetic implants, IV access devices, renal dialysis, and immunocompromised states. The default in every group is no prophylaxis.

workflows.title: Total joint replacement: no routine prophylaxis
workflows.overview:
Patients with total joint replacements are commonly referred to dental colleagues with verbal or written requests for antibiotic prophylaxis before treatment. The FDS-AMP recommendation, aligned with BSAC, is that this is not required.

## 1. Identify the patient at the visit

- Take the medical history at every recall; note hip, knee, shoulder or other joint replacements
- Date of replacement and operating team can be useful but does not change the recommendation
- Note who has advised the patient (often the orthopaedic surgeon or GP)

## 2. The default position

- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for dental procedures in patients with joint replacements**
- The hypothesis that oral bacteria cause prosthetic joint infections is **unproven** and rests on anecdotal case reports
- A systematic review of nine studies and additional literature concluded that there is **no evidence that use of antimicrobial prophylaxis reduces the incidence of joint infection**
- BSAC advises that patients with prosthetic joint implants (including total hip replacements) do not require antimicrobial prophylaxis for dental treatment

## 3. Manage the conversation when a surgeon or patient insists

1. **Acknowledge** the request and the source (orthopaedic team, GP, patient's own preference)
2. **Share the evidence**: no proven causal link, no benefit from prophylaxis, real harms (anaphylaxis, *C. difficile*, resistance)
3. **Refer back** to FDS-AMP and BSAC guidance; offer to send the recommendation to the requesting surgeon if helpful
4. **Document** the conversation, the guidance referenced, and the agreed plan
5. If the orthopaedic team has explicit case-specific concerns (e.g. recent joint sepsis, immunosuppression alongside a joint replacement), liaise with them rather than blanket-prescribing

## 4. The high-value alternative

For every joint replacement patient, the actually useful clinical intervention is:

- **Establishing and maintaining good oral health** before any planned orthopaedic surgery and continuously afterwards
- Treating active dental infection promptly so the patient does not arrive at orthopaedic clinic with an unmanaged source of bacteraemia
- This protects the joint far more reliably than a single pre-procedure antibiotic dose ever could

## 5. Procedural decisions are unchanged

- Use standard dental treatment principles for the procedure itself
- Standard infection prevention and control suffices
- No special antibiotic regimens are required for any dental procedure on the basis of the joint alone

workflows.title: Other prosthetic implants, IV access devices and renal dialysis: also no routine prophylaxis
workflows.overview:
FDS-AMP groups together a series of patient categories where the same recommendation applies: no routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures. Each rests on the same evidence base: an absence of demonstrated metastatic infection from dental procedures.

## 1. Miscellaneous prosthetic implants

Includes **penile implants, breast implants, cardiac pacemakers and intraocular implants**. These have **never been considered susceptible to infection** as a result of invasive dental procedures, and there is no strong evidence to support that they are.

- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended** for dental procedures in patients with cardiac pacemakers, penile, breast or intra-ocular implants
- Treat as a routine dental patient; standard infection control suffices

## 2. Intravenous access devices

Includes **central intravenous lines, indwelling catheters** for parenteral nutrition or chemotherapy, and **catheters for haemodialysis**.

- There is **no scientific evidence** of infection of these devices arising from invasive dental procedures
- BSAC recommends that antimicrobial prophylaxis is not required for dental treatment
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not required** for dental procedures in patients with intravenous access devices

## 3. Renal dialysis

Covers patients on **haemodialysis** (vascular access via fistula, graft or catheter) and **peritoneal dialysis**.

- Evidence is lacking; a theoretical risk of secondary infection of vascular graft sites has been hypothesised but not demonstrated
- There is **no clear evidence of metastatic infections** resulting from dental procedures in patients receiving renal dialysis
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis for patients undergoing renal dialysis is not normally recommended** for dental procedures

### Dialysis: caveats and clinical advice

- Consider advice on antimicrobial prophylaxis from the **renal specialist if there are co-morbidities** that change the calculus
- Stress the importance of **good oral health** with the patient
- Provide oral hygiene instruction and dietary advice
- Consider the need for **more regular recall** examinations
- Schedule treatment around dialysis sessions where practical (typically the day after rather than the day of dialysis, when bleeding tendency is lowest)

## 4. The single common rule

Across all four categories — miscellaneous implants, IV access devices, dialysis, and joint replacements — the FDS-AMP position is the same: **no routine prophylaxis**. Antimicrobials are reserved for treating established infection, not for prevention based on a non-cardiac device or condition alone.

## 5. When something does change the answer

- **Cardiac risk groups** for IE (covered separately under SDCEP IE prophylaxis): manage on the cardiac pathway, not on the device pathway
- **Established infection** at the dental site: treat the infection on its own merits using the acute-infection pathway
- **Combined risk** (e.g. a dialysis patient with a cardiac valve replacement) is managed on whichever pathway recommends prophylaxis, not on summation

workflows.title: Immunocompromised patients: aggressive treatment of infection, but no routine prophylaxis
workflows.overview:
Immune function may be impaired by leukaemia, immunosuppressive drugs after organ transplantation, lymphomas, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, poorly controlled diabetes and HIV. These patients are susceptible to opportunistic infections, but the FDS-AMP recommendation across the categories is still **no routine prophylaxis**.

The message is two-sided: do not over-prescribe prophylaxis, but **treat established infection aggressively and in liaison with the patient's specialist**.

## 1. The principle that runs through the whole section

Prompt, aggressive management of dental infections in this group is imperative and should be carried out in conjunction with the patient's specialist. There is **no evidence** to support increased risk of infection from dental procedures or increased risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) arising as a result of dental procedures in these patients.

## 2. Diabetes

- Well-controlled Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes are **not** a risk for postoperative surgical complications
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended routinely** for diabetic patients undergoing dental procedures
- Take a comprehensive history including control of diabetes; ensure the patient will not undergo hypoglycaemia on the day of treatment
- **Avoid aspirin and corticosteroids** as they may interact with hypoglycaemic medication
- Refer for specialist advice if there are other significant co-morbidities

## 3. HIV

- The majority of HIV-infected patients are medically stable; their dental care is shaped by non-HIV co-morbidities, not HIV itself
- Infection rates following dental procedures are comparable with non-HIV patients
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not routinely recommended** for HIV patients undergoing dental procedures, including in those with low CD4+ counts (<200 cells/mm³)
- **Severe neutropenia (<500 cells/mm³)**, which affects less than 1% of HIV-infected patients, should prompt discussion with the patient's haematologist before invasive procedures

## 4. Chemotherapy

- Establish good oral health **before** chemotherapy and delay elective treatment during it
- Infections of dental origin should be **aggressively managed** by removal of the cause and appropriate antimicrobials, in consultation with the oncologist
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not normally recommended** for dental procedures in patients undergoing chemotherapy
- Treat outside the chemotherapy cycle where possible

## 5. Radiotherapy and ORN

- Routine prophylactic antimicrobials for dental extractions to prevent osteoradionecrosis are not supported
- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis may be recommended for dental extractions following an assessment of the risk of developing ORN** (conditional recommendation, very low evidence)
- Patients who have undergone radiotherapy to the area of the extraction should be **referred for specialist management**
- Plan extractions and complete healing **before** radiotherapy where possible

## 6. Solid organ transplants

- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not routinely required** for patients with solid organ transplants prior to interventive dental procedures
- No dental treatment beyond stabilisation for emergencies for the **first 6 months** after transplant surgery
- Discuss overall health and the need for prophylaxis on a case-by-case basis with the medical or surgical team

## 7. Haemopoietic and lymphoid tumours

- **Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not routinely recommended** for dental procedures in these patients
- Best managed by specialists; consult the haematologist or transplant team for risk assessment of any invasive dental procedure during treatment
- Dental assessment and treatment should be **prior to chemotherapy and stem cell treatment**

## 8. Common ground across all groups

1. **No routine prophylaxis** for any of the categories above
2. **Treat established infection promptly and aggressively**, with antibiotics where indicated, in consultation with the patient's specialist
3. **Time elective dental treatment** to the patient's medical pathway: pre-chemotherapy, between cycles, before radiotherapy, after the first 6 transplant months
4. **Stress oral hygiene and prevention** as the durable contribution
5. **Refer** when in doubt; medically complex patients are often best managed by secondary or community dental services with specialist input

firstPrinciples.title: There is no evidence that dental procedures cause prosthetic joint infections, which is why prophylaxis is not recommended
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The orthopaedic team and patient sometimes still expect cover, but the evidence base does not support a causal link from oral bacteria to artificial joint infection.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the systematic review showed

A systematic review of nine studies and the supporting literature concluded that there was no evidence that use of antimicrobial prophylaxis reduces the incidence of joint infection [1]. The hypothesis that oral bacteria lead to prosthetic joint replacement infections is unproven and rests on anecdotal case reports [2].

## What BSAC and FDS-AMP recommend

Both the British Society for Antimicrobial Chemotherapy and FDS-AMP recommend against prophylaxis: antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for dental procedures in patients with joint replacements [3]. The agreement of national prescribing bodies makes this a position the GDP can defend confidently with a referring orthopaedic surgeon.

## What this changes in clinic

When a joint replacement patient or their orthopaedic team requests cover, the dentist's job is to acknowledge the request, share the evidence, and document the decision. The high-value clinical move is not the antibiotic but maintaining good oral health throughout the joint replacement journey. If the orthopaedic team has case-specific concerns rather than a blanket request, liaise directly rather than blanket-prescribing.

firstPrinciples.title: Pacemakers, breast implants, penile implants and intra-ocular implants do not need dental prophylaxis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Non-cardiac prosthetic implants of all kinds attract the same myth as joint replacements, and the FDS-AMP position is the same: not susceptible, no prophylaxis.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A category that has never been considered susceptible

FDS-AMP groups together patients with penile, breast, cardiac pacemaker and intraocular implants and reports that these have never been considered susceptible to infection as a result of invasive dental procedures, with no strong evidence to support that they are [1]. The recommendation flows directly: antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for dental procedures in patients with cardiac pacemakers, penile, breast or intra-ocular implants [2].

## Why pacemakers in particular often get confused

A cardiac pacemaker is a cardiovascular device, but it is not the kind of cardiac risk group that justifies IE prophylaxis. Pacemakers themselves do not get seeded by oral bacteraemia in the way that prosthetic valves do. The sorting question for the dentist is whether the patient sits in an IE-risk category for separate reasons (a coexisting valve replacement, for example), not whether they have a cardiac device.

## How this lands in practice

For a routine dental patient with one of these implants and no other relevant medical history, treatment proceeds with standard infection prevention and control. No special antibiotic regimen is required on the basis of the implant alone.

firstPrinciples.title: Renal dialysis patients do not need routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: End-stage renal disease patients carry significant cardiovascular risk and vascular access devices, but the dental procedure itself does not seed metastatic infection.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the theoretical concern is

The vascular access used for dialysis (fistula, vascular graft, catheter) carries a theoretical risk that grafts of collagen or polyurethane may be vulnerable to secondary infection from a dental procedure [1]. This is a hypothesis based on biomaterial behaviour, not on observed outcomes.

## What the actual evidence shows

There is no clear evidence of metastatic infections resulting from dental procedures in patients receiving renal dialysis, despite the well-known systemic complications of end-stage renal disease [2]. BSAC recommends prophylaxis is not required, and FDS-AMP makes the same recommendation [3].

## What the dentist should still do

The absence of prophylaxis does not mean there is nothing for the dentist to do. Dialysis patients benefit from oral hygiene instruction, dietary advice, more frequent recall, and scheduling treatment around dialysis sessions to manage bleeding risk. Where co-morbidities change the picture, advice from the renal specialist is appropriate.

firstPrinciples.title: In immunocompromised patients aggressive treatment of established infection matters more than prophylaxis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The clinical instinct that immunocompromised patients need cover for any procedure is the wrong instinct; the actual lever is fast, decisive treatment when infection appears.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The two-sided message

FDS-AMP states that prompt, aggressive management of dental infections in this group is imperative and should be carried out in conjunction with the patient's specialist [1]. At the same time, there is no evidence to support increased risk of infection from dental procedures or increased risk of surgical site infections in immunocompromised patients [2].

## How that plays out across subgroups

In diabetes, well-controlled Type 1 and Type 2 are not a risk for postoperative surgical complications, and prophylactic antimicrobials should not be prescribed other than where they would be indicated in a non-diabetic patient [3]. In HIV, infection rates after dental procedures are comparable with non-HIV patients, and prophylaxis is not routinely recommended even at low CD4+ counts. In chemotherapy and solid organ transplants the same pattern repeats: no routine prophylaxis, but aggressive treatment of established infection in consultation with the patient's specialist.

## What this changes for the GDP

A medically complex patient in the chair is not a reason to reach for a script. The right reflexes are establishing good oral health before medical treatment starts, scheduling dental work around the patient's medical pathway, treating established infection promptly with antimicrobials and source control, and consulting the specialist when complications stack up.

firstPrinciples.title: Post-radiotherapy extractions are the one immunocompromised situation where prophylaxis may be considered, after specialist risk assessment
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Radiotherapy carries a long-tail risk of osteoradionecrosis, which is the only setting in this section where FDS-AMP allows prophylaxis to enter the conversation, and only conditionally.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why ORN sits apart

Osteoradionecrosis is an area of exposed devitalised irradiated bone that fails to heal for three months or longer. A systematic review reports an incidence of around 7% for extractions in irradiated jaws, reducing to 6% with prophylactic antimicrobials [1]. The risk persists for years after radiotherapy, but is almost non-existent for extractions outside the field of irradiation [2].

## What FDS-AMP allows

Unlike every other subgroup in chapter 13.6, the recommendation for radiotherapy is conditional rather than negative: antimicrobial prophylaxis may be recommended for dental extractions following an assessment of the risk of developing ORN [3]. That assessment is the work of a specialist with access to the radiation records of dosage and field.

## What the GDP should do

For a patient who has had head and neck radiotherapy and now needs an extraction, the right action is to refer for specialist management rather than to extract in primary care with empirical antibiotic cover. Antimicrobial prophylaxis is given where clearly indicated by that assessment, alongside long-term follow-up after extraction.

firstPrinciples.title: Antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for dental procedures to prevent MRONJ
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Patients on anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication carry a small risk of MRONJ from dental procedures involving bone, but covering them prophylactically does not reduce that risk and adds antibiotic harm.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The size of the underlying risk

Estimates of MRONJ risk vary from 0.1% to 2% depending on drug regimen and medical diagnosis [1]. The risk is small in absolute terms, particularly for non-malignant indications, and antibiotic prophylaxis has not been shown to reduce it.

## The recommendation that follows

There are no RCTs investigating the efficacy of antimicrobial prophylaxis in preventing MRONJ in dental patients undergoing procedures involving bone. FDS-AMP advises balancing the very low risk of MRONJ against the side effects, toxicity and resistance consequences of antimicrobials [2]. The resulting recommendation is direct: antimicrobial prophylaxis is not recommended for dental procedures to prevent MRONJ [3].

## What actually reduces MRONJ risk

The interventions that do reduce MRONJ risk are pre-medication dental assessment, remedial treatment and preventive care; ongoing risk discussion with the patient; specialist referral for medically complex cases; healing review at around 8 weeks. None of these are pre-emptive antibiotics. The MRONJ pathway is captured in detail by the SDCEP MRONJ guidance, and that pathway also does not include routine prophylactic antimicrobials.

firstPrinciples.title: Solid organ transplant patients should have stabilisation only for the first 6 months after surgery
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Maximal immunosuppression sits in the first months after transplant, which is why elective dental treatment waits and emergency-only stabilisation is the norm.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why timing matters

The transplant patient is at greater risk of infection immediately following transplant because of maximal immunosuppression, and remains immunosuppressed indefinitely on antirejection medication [1]. Risk is highest when immunosuppression is heaviest, which in practice is the early post-transplant window.

## What FDS-AMP advises

FDS-AMP advises no dental treatment beyond stabilisation for emergencies for the first 6 months after transplant surgery, with overall health, dental treatment and any need for antimicrobial prophylaxis discussed case-by-case with the medical or surgical team [2]. Routine prophylactic antimicrobials are not required [3], but the planning of treatment timing is the actual lever.

## What this means for the GDP

Elective treatment is timed to the patient's medical pathway: dental health assessment and treatment ideally before the transplant, then a 6-month minimum window of emergency-only care, then case-by-case decision-making with the transplant team afterwards. Established dental infection in the early post-transplant period is treated promptly and aggressively with antimicrobials and source control, in liaison with the transplant team, rather than delayed.

workflows.title: Oral candidosis: identify the form, address predisposing factors, then antifungal
workflows.overview:
Oral candidosis is most often caused by Candida albicans. Carriage in the oral cavity is observed in up to 65% of mouths, with higher levels in young children and denture wearers. Recurrent infections flag underlying drivers that the dentist should address before reaching for an antifungal.

## 1. Identify the clinical form

### Pseudomembranous candidosis (thrush)
- Creamy white plaques on any oral mucosa or pharynx
- Diagnostically, the plaques can be **dislodged to leave raw bleeding mucosa**

### Erythematous candidosis (antibiotic sore mouth, acute atrophic candidosis)
- Red mucosa, often painful
- Typically associated with broad-spectrum antimicrobials or steroid inhalers

### Chronic hyperplastic candidosis (candidal leukoplakia)
- Clearly defined, fixed, raised white patch, sometimes speckled or nodular
- Classically at the commissures
- **Refer for specialist management** — this is considered a potentially malignant lesion and a diagnostic biopsy is required

### Denture stomatitis (chronic erythematous candidosis)
- Inflammation on the denture-bearing maxillary mucosa
- Often asymptomatic

### Angular cheilitis
- Cracking and inflammation of the angles of the mouth
- In **denture wearers**, usually fungal Candida (with a palatal reservoir from associated denture stomatitis)
- In **non-denture wearers**, more likely staphylococcal or streptococcal

## 2. Look for predisposing factors

Always relevant; sometimes managing them alone is curative.

- **Physiological**: elderly, infants, pregnancy
- **Local**: dry mouth, radiotherapy, poor oral hygiene, oral appliance wear, smoking
- **Medical**: antimicrobial therapy, systemic and inhaled steroids, immunosuppressive medication
- **Nutritional**: iron, folate, vitamin B12 deficiency, anaemia
- **Systemic**: endocrine disorders including diabetes
- **Immune**: HIV, AIDS
- **Malignancy**: acute leukaemia, agranulocytosis
- **Dry mouth**: radiation, drug therapy, Sjögren's syndrome

For inhaled steroids, advise rinsing and gargling with water immediately after use and using a spacer device.

## 3. Pseudomembranous and erythematous candidosis: drug choices

### Nystatin
- **Adults and children 1 month-18 years**: **100,000 units oral suspension four times a day after food for 7 days**, or continued for **2 days after lesions have healed**
- Advise rinsing the liquid around the mouth and holding it against the lesions for **5 minutes** before spitting out; avoid rinsing, eating or drinking immediately after use

### Or miconazole oromucosal gel
- **Adults**: apply **2.5 ml of oral gel** to the affected area **four times a day after food**, retain near the lesion before swallowing; use for **at least 7 days**, after lesions have healed or symptoms have cleared
- **Children 1-23 months**: 1.25 ml four times a day, smeared inside the mouth after feeds, continued for at least 7 days after lesions have healed
- **Children 2-17 years**: adult dose

### Or fluconazole (severe, extensive, or topical failed)
- **Adults**: **50 mg orally once a day for 7-14 days** (max 14 days unless severely immunocompromised); increased to 100 mg a day for unusually difficult infections
- **Children 12-17 years**: 50 mg once a day for 7-14 days
- **Children 1 month-11 years**: 3-6 mg/kg oral suspension on day 1 then 3 mg/kg (max 100 mg) daily for 7-14 days

## 4. Denture stomatitis: local measures lead

Address the denture, not just the candida.

1. **Strict denture hygiene** — chemical cleaning (hypochlorite for non-metal dentures, or chlorhexidine) plus mechanical cleansing twice a day
2. **Leave dentures out at night**
3. **Leave dentures out** whenever feasible during the day
4. **Tissue conditioners or soft linings** to manage trauma from poorly fitting dentures while planning new ones

Miconazole gel is a useful adjunct, especially before taking impressions for new dentures (5-10 ml applied to the fitting surface of the upper denture four times a day, until 48 hours after lesions resolve). Systemic antifungals are reserved for unresponsive infections, usually associated with underlying systemic factors.

## 5. Angular cheilitis

Manage predisposing factors first (treat the palatal candida reservoir if denture stomatitis is present, replace ill-fitting dentures, restore occlusal face height where lost).

- **Miconazole 2% cream** twice a day for 10 days or until lesions heal — first choice, covers both Candida and Gram-positive cocci
- **Sodium fusidate** ointment three to four times a day for around 7 days — when proven staphylococcal
- **Miconazole + hydrocortisone** cream (wet surfaces) or ointment (dry surfaces) twice a day for **maximum 7 days** — for unresponsive cases

## 6. Drug interactions and cautions

- **Miconazole** absorbs systemically even from topical use — **avoid in patients on warfarin** (anticoagulant effect potentiated) **or statins**
- **Fluconazole** — same warfarin and statin contraindication; max 14 days unless severely immunocompromised, in which case refer for specialist management
- **Nystatin** is not absorbed and is the safer choice when miconazole is contraindicated
- For prolonged courses or higher doses (e.g. immunocompromised) monitor liver and renal function

## 7. Refer when

- No response to local measures and a course of antifungal
- No identifiable cause
- Suspected chronic hyperplastic candidosis (potentially malignant)
- Severely immunocompromised patient with severe disease
- Children unresponsive to local measures and topical antifungal
- Angular cheilitis suggesting a haematinic deficiency or undiagnosed diabetes

workflows.title: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis: supportive care, with aciclovir for severe cases
workflows.overview:
Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) and most commonly presents in young children. The incubation period is approximately five days and infection can be subclinical. Most cases are managed with supportive care; aciclovir is reserved for severe cases.

## 1. Recognise the picture

- Young child (most cases) with widespread, painful intraoral vesicles and ulcers, including the gingival margin
- Generalised gingival inflammation, often the most striking feature
- Pyrexia, malaise, regional lymphadenopathy
- Fluid intake compromised by oral pain, with risk of dehydration
- Adult cases occur but are less common; tend to be more severe and prolonged

## 2. Full case assessment

In severe cases, perform a full case assessment to identify the patients who need more than supportive care:

- **Raised temperature** — quantify it, do not just note "febrile"
- **Swollen lymph nodes**
- **Malaise** and reduced oral intake
- **Dehydration** — particularly important in small children
- **Immunocompromise** — current diagnosis or treatment

Patients in this severe group may require systemic intravenous antiviral therapy and should be **referred for urgent hospital treatment**.

## 3. Supportive measures (the entire treatment in mild cases)

Management of oral viral infections is symptomatic and usually involves:

- **Rest**
- **Plenty of fluids** — push hydration explicitly
- **Soft diet**
- **Antipyretic analgesics** (paracetamol; ibuprofen is also useful where appropriate following NICE mild-to-moderate pain guidance)
- **Antimicrobial mouthwash** to reduce secondary infection — chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide are suitable
- **Benzydamine mouthwash** can give some pain relief

## 4. Decide if aciclovir is needed

Antivirals are **only recommended for severe cases** of primary herpetic stomatitis (strong recommendation, low quality evidence). The evidence supporting aciclovir is described as weak but consistent: it can reduce the number of oral lesions, prevent new extraoral lesions, decrease difficulty in eating and drinking, and reduce hospital admission for children under 6 years.

## 5. Aciclovir regimen

### Adults
- **Aciclovir 200 mg five times a day for 5 days** (longer if new lesions appear during treatment or if healing is incomplete)

### Children
- **1-23 months**: **100 mg five times a day for 5 days** (longer if new lesions appear during treatment or if healing is incomplete)
- **2-17 years**: **200 mg five times a day for 5 days** (longer if new lesions appear during treatment or if healing is incomplete)

## 6. Hydration and safeguarding

- A child who refuses fluids because of oral pain is at real risk of dehydration; the threshold to refer for hospital management is low
- Ensure parents have realistic information about how to push fluids: cold drinks, ice lollies, soft foods
- Use rapid PCR detection where indicated, particularly in immunocompromised patients
- Review the patient; refer for specialist input if there is failure to respond, to exclude an underlying systemic condition

## 7. After the acute episode

- Educate the patient or parent that the virus remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion
- Approximately one third of people will develop herpes labialis from later reactivation of the virus
- Reassure that recurrent cold sores do not need routine topical antiviral treatment; topical preparations are not routinely recommended for recurrent HSV
- Patients who are immunocompromised, with frequent or persistent recurrent HSV, atypical lesions or an uncertain diagnosis should be referred for specialist management

firstPrinciples.title: Oral candidosis is rarely a primary disease; the predisposing factor is usually the cause
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Candida species are commensals in most mouths. Symptomatic infection appears when something tilts the local or systemic balance, which means the predisposing factor is the higher-yield target than the antifungal.
firstPrinciples.body:
## High background carriage

Candida species carriage in the oral cavity, particularly on the dorsum of the tongue, is observed in up to 65% of patients' mouths, with higher colonisation levels in young children and denture wearers [1]. The presence of yeast in the mouth is the norm, not the disease.

## Predisposing factors as the actual driver

FDS-AMP lists the predisposing factors that tilt commensal carriage into infection: physiological (elderly, infants, pregnancy), local (dry mouth, radiotherapy, poor oral hygiene, oral appliance wear, smoking), medical (antimicrobial therapy, systemic and inhalation steroid therapy, immunosuppressive medication), nutritional (iron, folate, vit B12 deficiencies, anaemia), systemic (endocrine disorders including diabetes), immune disorders (HIV, AIDS), malignancy and dry mouth from any cause [2]. Recurrent infections are problematic in patients where the risk factors or underlying disease cannot be readily eliminated or controlled [3].

## What this changes in clinic

The first move on a candidosis diagnosis is not to write the antifungal but to map the predisposing factor. Inhaled steroid technique, dry mouth, smoking, denture hygiene, undiagnosed diabetes, haematinic deficiency: each of these has a specific intervention that may resolve the candidosis without a script. The antifungal is layered on top once the underlying driver is being addressed.

firstPrinciples.title: Miconazole and fluconazole interact with warfarin and statins; nystatin does not
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Topical-looking antifungals can have systemic consequences in polypharmacy patients, which is why the warfarin and statin question matters before any candida prescription.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why miconazole behaves systemically

Miconazole oromucosal gel is applied to the mouth, but it is absorbed sufficiently to interact with cytochrome P450-metabolised drugs, particularly warfarin (potentiation of anticoagulant effect, INR rise, bleeding risk) and statins (rhabdomyolysis risk via raised statin levels) [1]. Fluconazole shares the same CYP-mediated interaction profile.

## Nystatin as the safer alternative

Nystatin is not absorbed from the gut, so it does not produce the same systemic interactions [2]. When miconazole is contraindicated, the standard substitution is nystatin oral suspension 100,000 units four times a day. The trade-off is that nystatin requires a deliberate technique (rinse, hold against the lesion for five minutes, do not eat or drink immediately afterwards) to deliver enough contact time at the lesion.

## What this means for the prescription decision

For any patient on warfarin or a statin, the candidosis prescription defaults to nystatin first or fluconazole only if the systemic risk is acknowledged and managed (INR monitoring, statin review). For an angular cheilitis patient on warfarin, miconazole 2% cream is also out, even at the corners of the mouth.

firstPrinciples.title: Chronic hyperplastic candidosis is a potentially malignant lesion and is a referral, not a script
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The white patch that cannot be wiped off is not the same disease as the white plaque that can, and the prognostic implications are very different.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why hyperplastic candidosis sits apart

Chronic hyperplastic candidosis presents as a clearly defined, fixed, raised white patch that may be speckled or nodular, classically at the commissures [1]. Unlike the wipeable plaques of pseudomembranous candidosis, the hyperplastic lesion does not come off and often coexists with epithelial dysplasia.

## What FDS-AMP advises

Specialist management is necessary because this is generally considered to be a potentially malignant lesion and a diagnostic biopsy is required [2]. The timing of antifungal treatment relative to biopsy is itself a specialist decision: many specialists treat the candida first to avoid over-reporting dysplasia caused by candidal infiltration, while others biopsy first then treat then re-biopsy [3].

## The lesson for the GDP

A fixed white patch at the commissure that does not wipe off does not earn a course of nystatin. It earns a referral. Treating empirically with antifungal in primary care risks masking a potentially malignant lesion and delaying biopsy.

firstPrinciples.title: Denture stomatitis is treated by changing how the denture is worn, not by an antifungal
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Denture stomatitis is one of the few oral candidoses where the predisposing factor is fully under the patient's behavioural control, so management focuses there first.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the source tells the patient to do

FDS-AMP lists local measures as the primary treatment of denture stomatitis: strict denture hygiene using regular chemical (hypochlorite for non-metal dentures, or chlorhexidine) and mechanical cleansing twice a day, leaving dentures out at night, leaving dentures out whenever feasible during the day, and using tissue conditioners or soft linings to minimise mucosal trauma in poorly fitting dentures prior to construction of new dentures [1].

## Where the antifungal sits

A meta-analysis of RCTs found no statistically significant difference between antifungal treatment and disinfection methods for clinical and microbiological outcomes in denture stomatitis [2]. Antifungal therapy adds value primarily as an adjunct to local measures and especially before constructing new dentures, where reducing palatal inflammation matters for impression-taking. Systemic antifungals are reserved for unresponsive infections, usually associated with underlying systemic factors such as immunosuppression or diabetes [3].

## What this changes for the GDP

The right intervention for the patient with a red palate under their upper denture is not a fluconazole script. It is denture hygiene instruction, the explicit advice to take dentures out overnight, and a check on the fit of the prosthesis. The antifungal is layered on if local measures fail or impressions for new dentures are imminent.

firstPrinciples.title: Angular cheilitis aetiology splits along denture-wear status
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The simple clinical question "do you wear dentures" predicts whether the corner of the mouth is more likely fungal or bacterial, and therefore which agent comes first.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A clean clinical split

Angular cheilitis has a multifactorial aetiology and may be caused by both yeasts (Candida spp.) and bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus and beta-haemolytic streptococci) as interacting infective factors. In patients who do not wear dentures, bacterial infections with staphylococci and/or streptococci are more likely to be cultured from the lesions [1]. In denture wearers, the lesion typically connects to a palatal candida reservoir from associated denture stomatitis.

## The matching first-line agents

FDS-AMP recommends miconazole cream as first choice because it has antifungal activity and some activity against Gram-positive cocci, covering both ends of the aetiological split in one tube [2]. Where the lesion is proven staphylococcal, sodium fusidate ointment is indicated, applied three to four times a day usually for 7 days [3]. For unresponsive cases, miconazole with hydrocortisone is added for a maximum of 7 days.

## What the dentist should also do

Manage the predisposing factor: treat any intraoral candida reservoir at the same time, replace ill-fitting dentures, and restore occlusal face height where it has been lost. Persistent angular cheilitis without an obvious denture or candida cause should prompt blood tests to look for haematinic deficiency or undiagnosed diabetes.

firstPrinciples.title: Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis is a hydration diagnosis as much as a viral one
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The clinical risk in young children with primary HSV is not the virus itself but the dehydration that follows when oral pain stops fluid intake.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the supportive treatment is for

FDS-AMP frames management of oral viral infections as symptomatic and centred on rest, plenty of fluids, soft diet, antipyretic analgesics, antimicrobial mouthwash to reduce secondary infection, and benzydamine mouthwash for pain relief [1]. Each of these measures targets either fluid intake itself or the pain that prevents it.

## When to escalate

In severe cases, full case assessment is required to look for raised temperature, swollen lymph nodes, malaise, dehydration, or immunocompromise. These patients may require systemic intravenous antiviral therapy and should be referred for urgent hospital treatment [2].

## What the antiviral does and does not do

A systematic review suggests that there is some weak evidence of aciclovir being an effective treatment in reducing the number of oral lesions, preventing the development of new extraoral lesions, decreasing the number of individuals with difficulties experienced in eating and drinking, and reducing hospital admission for children under 6 years [3]. The benefit is real but modest, and the recommendation is therefore that antivirals are only recommended for severe cases. The dehydration safety net stays in place regardless of whether aciclovir is prescribed.

Chlorhexidine or hydrogen peroxide are suitable agents. The use of benzydamine mouthwash may provide some pain relief

firstPrinciples.title: After primary HSV, about a third of people get herpes labialis from later reactivation, but topical antivirals are not routinely recommended
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The latent virus in the trigeminal ganglion sets up a long tail of recurrent cold sores, but the routine over-the-counter and prescribed topical antivirals offer marginal benefit at best.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What latency means clinically

Following primary herpetic gingivostomatitis infection, herpes simplex remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion. Approximately one third of people develop herpes labialis and a secondary infection from reactivation of the virus [1]. The patient's lifelong cold sore tendency is set in childhood by the primary episode.

## Why topical antivirals are not routinely recommended

A systematic review of 12 RCTs comparing topical aciclovir or penciclovir with placebo in healthy patients found that these agents may reduce pain and healing time, but the results of the studies were inconsistent and of marginal clinical importance [2]. FDS-AMP therefore states that topical antiviral preparations are not routinely recommended for herpes simplex infections [3].

## What the clinical advice is

For the routine cold sore in a healthy patient, reassurance, advice on minimising risk of transmission, avoiding trigger factors and over-the-counter lip barriers or moisturising balms is enough. Oral antivirals are considered for severe, frequent or persistent lesions. Patients with immunocompromise, atypical lesions or uncertain diagnosis are referred for specialist management.

workflows.title: Decide whether to extract a compromised first permanent molar
workflows.overview:
## 1. Recognise the problem

A child presenting with one or more compromised first permanent molars (FPM) of uncertain prognosis carries a burden of disease that can lead to sensitivity, pain, complex restorations or extractions and disruption of the functional occlusion. Two anchoring rules from the RCS guideline:

- Elective extraction must always be considered **within the context of the patient and their underlying occlusion**
- Treatment-planning decisions should ideally be made following input from **both the GDP or paediatric dentist and a specialist orthodontist**

## 2. Settle the immediate clinical picture

If the child is in pain or has acute pathology, manage that first. Enforced extraction may have to happen before any ideal timing or balancing can be planned. Future planning is then revisited once the acute phase is controlled.

If there are no immediate needs, **stabilise or temporise** the compromised FPM where possible to allow time for specialist input and a proper plan.

## 3. Take a full assessment

Record:

1. Immediate symptoms related to the compromised FPM
2. Accurate prognosis of each affected tooth, plus an appraisal of likely future symptoms
3. The child's **capacity** to receive complex care, including surgical, restorative and orthodontic treatment, with input from the patient, guardians and the GDP or paediatric dentist
4. Availability of services, including location and financial burden
5. The overall occlusion or malocclusion (a detailed dental and orthodontic assessment)
6. The aspirations and values of the child and parent regarding present care and the burden of future care

## 4. Imaging is mandatory

A full dental assessment must include a radiographic screen with a **Dental Panoramic Tomograph (DPT)** to check the presence, position and normal formation of the full developing permanent dentition. Without a recent DPT to assess SPM development and TPM presence, the interceptive guidance does **not** apply.

## 5. Weigh prognosis carefully

Evidence-based decisions on prognosis are difficult. Any restoration is likely to fail eventually, and MIH-affected teeth that look grossly intact may have opacities that break down later. Document any restorative work, including pre-operative photographs where possible, to support future planning.

## 6. Consider developmental versus chronological age

The developmental age of the patient may be very different to their chronological age. This must be considered before choosing a treatment that relies on the eruptive pathway of the adult dentition.

## 7. Branch by features of the occlusion

- **Significant mid-arch crowding** → may require **stabilisation** of the compromised FPM to avoid further space loss
- **Hypodontia** → may require **early extraction or restoration** of compromised teeth to manage the long-term occlusal platform
- **TPM present** → much more acceptable to extract a compromised FPM with uncertain prognosis (expectation of two molars per quadrant)
- **No TPM** → extraction risks leaving a single molar unit in that quadrant; needs a more detailed conversation between patient, dentist and orthodontist

## 8. Refer where possible

Referral to centres where combined orthodontic and paediatric services are available is the **gold standard**. Where this is not possible, the guideline supports the attending clinician to make the call.

## 9. Shared decision-making and consent

Communicate all options to the patient and parents or guardians:

- Some patients will prefer to lose a tooth rather than carry a lifetime burden of restorative repair
- Others will choose to maintain a tooth at all costs

Factor in whether treatment will be under **local anaesthetic, sedation or general anaesthetic**, especially if multi-stage. Outcomes are often not completely predictable and depend on favourable growth, which makes proper informed consent essential.

## 10. Treat as dynamic

Interceptive extraction in the developing dentition is a dynamic intervention requiring **professional supervision and careful review**. It should not be considered a one-off intervention.

workflows.title: Pick the ideal timing for first permanent molar extraction
workflows.overview:
## 1. Confirm the guideline applies

The timing guidance is **not** for use if:

- The SPM is already erupted (an erupted SPM in occlusion will not migrate mesially, so there is no advantage to an interceptive approach)
- A recent DPT to assess SPM development and TPM presence is not available
- Acute symptoms (pain, swelling, infection) are present and the FPM cannot be temporised

## 2. Use the radiographic predictors of successful SPM eruption

Classically the strongest predictor for successful eruption of the SPM after FPM removal, particularly in the lower arch, is **early mineralisation of the SPM bifurcation** seen on DPT. This may simply reflect the child's overall developmental stage. More recent work points to two further radiographic predictors:

- **Mesio-distal angulation of the SPM**
- **Presence of the TPM**

These predictive factors matter most after extraction of a **compromised lower FPM**; favourable eruption is much less of a concern after upper FPM extraction.

## 3. Aim for the developmental window

Extraction of the compromised FPM when the **SPM is developing, between 8 and 10 years**, appears to cause the least disruption to the occlusion. Falling outside that window has consequences, especially in the lower arch.

### Lower FPM extracted too early (before 8 years)
- The SPM and second premolar can drift into the extraction space
- Tipping, rotation and spacing may follow
- Poor occlusal contacts result

### Lower FPM extracted too late (during later stages of SPM eruption)
- Same problems: drift, tipping, rotation, spacing, poor contacts
- The chance to direct the SPM into a clean replacement position is lost

## 4. Factor in the TPM, even when uncertain

TPM development is usually evident radiographically by **8 years of age**, but it can vary widely and be significantly delayed. Treatment planning often has to happen before TPM presence is confirmed.

- **TPM present** → expectation of two molars per quadrant in good occlusion; extraction of a compromised FPM with uncertain prognosis is much more acceptable
- **No TPM** → reduced posterior occlusion possible, with unopposed teeth if a TPM exists in the opposing quadrant; needs a much more detailed conversation between patient, dentist and orthodontist

Interceptive FPM extraction can also improve the position of the TPM in both upper and lower jaws, which adds support to extraction in uncertain-prognosis cases.

## 5. Branch by arch

### Upper arch
- Unerupted SPM generally achieves a good occlusal position after extraction of a compromised upper FPM
- The upper SPM can be expected to drift mesially into contact with the second premolar
- If there is upper crowding, or space will be needed for class II correction, consider **temporising the FPM** until the SPM erupts, then placing a **palatal arch** on the erupted SPMs to maintain the FPM space
- Where appliance wear is not feasible, or urgent care under GA is required, plan space requirements and consider interceptive extraction of any other teeth (including assessing **upper canine** position) at the time of FPM removal
- For patients who can access specialist orthodontic care, **TADs and innovative fixed anchorage** have made the impact of upper FPM space loss much less significant

### Lower arch
- Occlusal outcomes are more variable and less predictable
- Timing of FPM extraction is therefore **more critical**
- Use **early mineralisation of the SPM bifurcation** and **SPM angulation** with **TPM presence** as the radiographic predictors
- Space requirements are often less demanding, depending on the underlying malocclusion

## 6. Review and adapt

At every stage and after each intervention, review the plan to reflect changes in the child's capacity, the family's wishes and the actual development of the dentition.

workflows.title: Decide on compensating and balancing extractions
workflows.overview:
## 1. Define the two terms precisely

The RCS guideline defines:

- **Compensating extraction** — removal of a FPM from the **opposing quadrant**
- **Balancing extraction** — removal of a FPM from the **opposite side of the same dental arch**

Getting these the right way round in the records and the conversation with the orthodontist matters; they answer different problems.

## 2. Compensating extraction (across the arches)

**Setting:** Enforced extraction of a **lower FPM** is required, and the question is whether to electively extract the sound **upper FPM** in the same quadrant.

**Historical rationale (Holm, 1970):** Compensating extraction was recommended to avoid over-eruption of an unopposed upper FPM, which can:

- Prevent desirable mesial movement of the erupting lower SPM
- Impede space closure in the lower arch
- Potentially induce other occlusal interferences

**Current evidence:** The risk of upper FPM over-eruption after lower FPM extraction is **small**. Available studies are retrospective cohorts with small samples.

**Recommendation:** When the enforced extraction of a lower FPM is required, the compensating extraction of a **sound upper FPM should not be routinely carried out** unless there is a clear occlusal requirement or a likelihood of the upper FPM being **unopposed for a significant period of time**.

## 3. Balancing extraction (within the same arch)

**Setting:** A FPM has been extracted on one side, and the question is whether to electively extract the sound contralateral FPM in the same arch to preserve symmetry.

**Historical rationale:** Balancing was recommended to **preserve arch symmetry**. Retrospective cohorts have suggested that unilateral FPM extraction can be associated with both skeletal and dental arch asymmetries.

**Current evidence:** Similar study designs suggest the **dental centreline** in either arch is unlikely to be affected.

**Recommendation:** Routine balancing extraction of a sound FPM to preserve a dental centreline is **not recommended unless part of a comprehensive orthodontic treatment plan**.

## 4. Apply at the chair

At the point of decision:

1. State out loud which extraction is being proposed, and which type it is (compensating or balancing)
2. Check it against the relevant recommendation
3. Justify and document any departure from the default
4. Where any non-routine extraction is being considered for symmetry or anchorage reasons, route the case through a specialist orthodontist as part of a wider treatment plan

## 5. Limits of the evidence

Most of the supporting work in this area is retrospective cohort studies, often with very small samples and incomplete reporting. Decisions should therefore be made cautiously, on the individual case, and in concert with an orthodontist whenever the indication is occlusal or aesthetic rather than urgent.
