firstPrinciples.title: FPM root completion is around 9 to 10 years
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Knowing when FPM development is complete helps the clinician reason about when interceptive extraction can be done early enough to influence the eruption of the second permanent molar.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A predictable developmental schedule

The first permanent molar is derived from the primary dental lamina, with evidence of early formation usually present by week 17 of gestation. Hard tissue formation is generally initiated by birth and coronal development is complete by the third year of life [1]. The FPM erupts around the age of 6 to 7 years, and root formation is complete by the age of 9 to 10 years [2].

## Why this matters at the chair

Interceptive timing guidance turns on the developmental stage of adjacent teeth, especially the SPM. Knowing the FPM's own schedule grounds those judgements: by the time the FPM is fully formed, the developing SPM is well into its own root formation and the radiographic checkpoints used to time extraction are already in play. The clinician planning a child's molar dentition is working inside this fixed schedule, not against it.

citations.quote: Hard tissue formation is generally initiated in these teeth by birth and coronal development is complete by the third year of life;
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Development of the first permanent molar

citations.quote: Root formation is complete by the age of 9-10 years (Berkovitz et al., 2017; Nanci, 2017);
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Development of the first permanent molar

firstPrinciples.title: FPM coronal mineralisation timing makes it vulnerable to enamel defects
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Because FPM enamel mineralises in the perinatal and infant period, any systemic insult during that window can leave defects that present clinically years later.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A susceptible window

The timing of coronal mineralisation makes FPM teeth susceptible to chronological and systemic enamel defects, which can lead to localised hypomineralisation or hypoplasia [1]. Coronal development is largely a perinatal and early-childhood process, so any systemic insult in that period can imprint on the enamel that erupts years later.

## Why this matters clinically

This is the developmental basis for why FPMs so often present compromised when the child reaches the dentist's chair. Caries on a structurally normal FPM is one problem; caries or post-eruptive breakdown on an FPM that was already hypomineralised is another, and the prognosis assessment has to factor that in. It also means a clinician seeing one defective FPM should look for matching defects in the other FPMs and the permanent incisors, since the same chronological insult would have hit those teeth at the same time.

citations.quote: The timing of coronal mineralisation makes FPM teeth susceptible to chronological and systemic enamel defects, which can lead to localised hypomineralisation and/or hypoplasia (Leppaniemi et al., 2001).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Development of the first permanent molar

firstPrinciples.title: MIH is a defined systemic enamel disorder of the FPM and incisors
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Molar-Incisor-Hypomineralisation is a recognised syndrome of demarcated qualitative enamel defects, not generic caries, and its enamel is prone to post-eruptive breakdown.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A distinct entity

Molar-Incisor-Hypomineralisation (MIH) is a systemic condition with a poorly understood aetiology, characterised by demarcated and qualitative enamel defects variably affecting the FPM and permanent incisor teeth [1]. The pattern is what gives the condition its name: the FPMs and the incisors are the teeth mineralising at the right developmental moment to be affected together.

## Why MIH changes the prognosis conversation

Post-eruptive breakdown of FPM coronal enamel is common in MIH and can lead to sensitivity, increased caries risk and challenging restorative care [2]. A grossly intact-looking MIH-affected tooth may have opacities that break down later, so a single early decision can become several future decisions. This is why MIH-affected children require careful treatment planning and specific care pathways, and why FPMs with MIH so often end up in the interceptive-extraction conversation rather than the routine restorative one.

citations.quote: Molar-Incisor-Hypomineralisation (MIH) is a systemic condition with a poorly understood aetiology, that is increasingly being seen and characterised by demarcated and qualitative enamel defects variably affecting the FPM and permanent incisor teeth (Jalevik, 2010; Kuhnisch et al., 2012),
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Why is the FPM a particular problem?

citations.quote: Post-eruptive breakdown of FPM coronal enamel is common and can lead to sensitivity, increased caries risk and challenging restorative care.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Why is the FPM a particular problem?

firstPrinciples.title: Caries in UK 15 year olds is still common despite long-term decline
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: FPM disease burden in children sits inside a national caries pattern where decline has plateaued, with around a third of older teenagers still carrying experience of dentinal caries.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The national picture

Caries experience has continually fallen in the permanent dentition of UK children over the last forty years, but the most recent data show that around one third of UK 15 year olds still have experience of caries into dentine in at least one of their permanent teeth [1]. The FPM is one of the first permanent teeth to erupt, and a degree of inaccessibility at the back of the mouth makes it susceptible to caries if the conditions are unfavourable.

## Why a GDP should remember the figure

It anchors the prevalence of compromised FPMs in actual numbers rather than impressions. When a child arrives with one or more questionable FPMs, that situation is not unusual within their cohort. Treating it as a routine clinical scenario, with a default to plan rather than react, is justified by how often it is encountered in normal NHS practice.

citations.quote: Whilst caries experience has continually fallen in the permanent dentition of UK children over the last forty years, the most recent data has demonstrated that around one third of UK 15 year-olds still have experience of caries into dentine in at least one of their permanent teeth (Child Dental Health Survey, 2013).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Why is the FPM a particular problem?

firstPrinciples.title: Extraction in the 8 to 10 year window minimises occlusal disruption
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: When the SPM is still developing, the extraction space is filled by predictable mesial drift; outside the window, the SPM and second premolar tend to tip and rotate into the gap.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The biological window

Extraction of the compromised FPM when the SPM is developing, between the ages of 8 and 10 years, appears to cause less disruption to the occlusion [1]. Within this window the SPM has enough developmental momentum to drift mesially in a controlled way and replace the FPM in good occlusal position.

## What goes wrong outside it

If the lower FPM is extracted before the age of 8 years, or during the later stages of SPM eruption, the SPM and second premolar can drift into the extraction space, tip, rotate and produce spacing in the dental arch with poor occlusal contacts [2]. The same biology that makes timing decisive also explains why the upper arch is more forgiving: the upper SPM tends to drift mesially into a good position regardless of the exact moment of FPM removal.

citations.quote: Extraction of the compromised FPM when the SPM is developing (between the ages of 8-10 years) appears to cause less disruption to the occlusion.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

citations.quote: If this window is not met and the lower FPM is extracted before the age of 8 years, or during the later stages of SPM eruption, the SPM and second premolar can drift into the extraction space, tip, rotate and produce spacing in the dental arch with poor occlusal contacts (Normando et al., 2010; Thilander et al., 1963; Thilander and Skagius, 1970; Thunold, 1970).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

firstPrinciples.title: SPM bifurcation mineralisation is the classical radiographic timing marker
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Early calcification of the SPM bifurcation on a panoramic radiograph signals readiness for FPM extraction with predictable spontaneous space closure, especially in the lower arch.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The classical sign

Radiographic evidence of a SPM within alveolar bone and early mineralisation of its bifurcation have been cited as predictors for successful eruption of this tooth following FPM extraction, particularly in the lower arch [1]. It is the marker the clinician looks for on the DPT before recommending interceptive extraction of a lower FPM.

## A useful caveat

The predictive value may simply reflect the developmental stage of the child rather than something specific to SPM development [1]. More recent work suggests that the **mesio-distal angulation of the SPM** and the **presence of the TPM** may be at least as important predictors of a favourable erupted occlusal position [2]. The bifurcation sign therefore remains useful, but is read alongside angulation and TPM presence, not in isolation.

citations.quote: Radiographic evidence of a SPM within alveolar bone and early mineralisation of its bifurcation have been cited as predictors for successful eruption of this tooth following FPM extraction, particularly in the lower arch (Normando et al., 2010; Thilander et al., 1963; Thilander and Skagius, 1970; Thunold, 1970). However, this might simply reflect the developmental stage of the child rather than anything specific to SPM development.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

citations.quote: More recent research has identified a predictive relationship relating to mesio-distal angulation of the SPM and presence of the TPM in terms of favourable SPM eruption (Patel et al., 2017).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

firstPrinciples.title: TPM presence is usually radiographically evident by 8 years, but variable
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The presence or absence of the third permanent molar is a key determinant of how acceptable FPM extraction is, but planning often has to happen before the radiograph can confirm it.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The radiographic timing

TPM development is usually evident radiographically by 8 years of age, but it can demonstrate wide variation and be delayed significantly [1]. Treatment planning often needs to be undertaken before the presence or absence of the TPM can be confirmed.

## How TPM status changes the decision

If a TPM is present and FPM interceptive extraction is carried out at the optimal time, or the patient is able to undergo orthodontic treatment, there is every expectation that the child will ultimately have two molars in each quadrant in good occlusion, which makes extracting a compromised FPM with uncertain prognosis much more acceptable [2]. Where there is no TPM, extraction of the FPM may leave the child with only one molar unit in the affected quadrant, possibly unopposed if TPMs are present in the opposing quadrant; this requires a more detailed conversation between patient, dentist and orthodontist [3]. Interceptive extraction itself can also improve the position of the TPM in both jaws, which adds to the case for removal in uncertain-prognosis situations.

citations.quote: TPM development is usually evident radiographically by 8 years of age, but it can demonstrate wide variation and be delayed significantly. This is unfortunate because treatment planning often needs to be undertaken before the presence or absence of the TPM can be confirmed.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

citations.quote: If a TPM is present and FPM interceptive extraction is carried out at the optimal time or the patient is able to undergo orthodontic treatment, there is every expectation that the child will ultimately have two molars in each quadrant in good occlusion; and therefore, in these circumstances, it is much more acceptable to extract a compromised FPM with an uncertain prognosis.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

citations.quote: Extraction of the FPM will potentially leave the child with only one molar unit in the affected quadrant, leading to a reduced posterior occlusion and possibly unopposed teeth, if TPM are present in the opposing quadrant. This situation requires a much more detailed conversation between patient, dentist and orthodontist.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

firstPrinciples.title: Lower arch outcomes after FPM extraction are less predictable than upper
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Spontaneous space closure is more reliable in the upper arch, which is why extraction timing matters most in the lower arch and why the radiographic predictors are weighted there.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why arches differ

In the upper arch, an unerupted SPM will generally achieve a good occlusal position following extraction of the compromised FPM, drifting mesially into contact with the second premolar [1]. In the lower arch, occlusal outcomes are more variable and less predictable, and the timing of FPM extraction is more critical to ensure successful eruption of the SPM [2].

## What this means for practice

This asymmetry is why the radiographic predictors (bifurcation mineralisation, SPM angulation, TPM presence) are most pertinent for compromised lower FPMs, and why favourable SPM eruption is much less of a concern after upper FPM extraction [3]. Practically, a GDP can be more relaxed about timing in the upper arch and should be more careful about it in the lower arch. The introduction of TADs and innovative fixed anchorage techniques has also softened the impact of upper FPM space loss in patients who can access specialist orthodontic care.

citations.quote: In the upper arch, an unerupted SPM will generally achieve a good occlusal position following extraction of the compromised FPM (Patel et al., 2017). The upper SPM can be expected to drift mesially into contact with the second premolar.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), General principles of management: upper arch

citations.quote: In the lower arch, occlusal outcomes are more variable and less predictable and the timing of FPM extraction is more critical to ensure successful eruption of the SPM (Plint, 1970; Teo et al., 2013; Thilander et al., 1963; Thilander and Skagius, 1970; Thunold, 1970).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), General principles of management: lower arch

citations.quote: These predictive factors are more pertinent following extraction of a compromised lower FPM, as favourable SPM eruption is less of a concern following extraction of a compromised upper FPM (Ay et al., 2006; Halicioglu et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2017; Williams and Hosila, 1976; Yavuz et al., 2006).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Predictors of successful SPM eruption following interceptive FPM removal

firstPrinciples.title: Routine compensating extraction of a sound upper FPM is not recommended
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: When a lower FPM has to come out, electively removing the sound upper opposing FPM is not the default; modern evidence puts the over-eruption risk lower than older guidance assumed.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the rule actually is

When the enforced extraction of a lower FPM is required, the compensating extraction of a sound upper FPM should not be routinely carried out unless there is a clear occlusal requirement or likelihood of the upper FPM being unopposed for a significant period of time [1]. The historical rationale was to avoid over-eruption of an unopposed upper FPM, which can prevent desirable mesial movement of the erupting lower SPM, impede space closure and induce other occlusal interferences.

## Why the recommendation softened

The evidence on which the historical recommendation rests is largely retrospective cohort studies, often with very small samples. Current evidence would suggest that the risk of upper FPM over-eruption as a consequence of lower FPM extraction is small [2]. The default position has therefore moved from prophylactic compensating extraction towards monitoring, with elective removal reserved for cases where the upper tooth is genuinely going to be unopposed for a long period or there is a defined occlusal need.

citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Should we provide balancing and compensating extractions?

citations.quote: Current evidence would suggest that the risk of upper FPM over-eruption as a consequence of lower FPM extraction is small (Jalevik and Moller, 2007; Mejare et al., 2005).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Should we provide balancing and compensating extractions?

firstPrinciples.title: Routine balancing extraction of a sound FPM is not recommended
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Removing the contralateral sound FPM purely to preserve dental centreline symmetry is not supported; the centreline is unlikely to be affected by unilateral extraction.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The recommendation

Routine balancing extraction of a sound FPM to preserve a dental centreline is not recommended unless part of a comprehensive orthodontic treatment plan [1]. Balancing was historically recommended to preserve arch symmetry, supported by retrospective cohort suggestions that unilateral FPM extraction can be associated with both skeletal and dental arch asymmetries.

## Why the centreline argument doesn't hold

Evidence from similar study designs suggests that the dental centreline in either arch is unlikely to be affected by unilateral FPM extraction [2]. The clinician's default is therefore to leave the contralateral sound FPM alone, and to fold any decision to remove it into a wider orthodontic plan rather than treating it as a routine occlusal hygiene measure.

citations.quote: Recommendation: Routine balancing extraction of a sound FPM to preserve a dental centreline is not recommended unless part of a comprehensive orthodontic treatment plan.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Should we provide balancing and compensating extractions?

citations.quote: Evidence from similar study designs suggests that the dental centreline in either arch is unlikely to be affected (Jalevik and Moller, 2007; Mejare et al., 2005).
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Should we provide balancing and compensating extractions?

firstPrinciples.title: FPM treatment planning needs combined GDP and orthodontic input
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Outcomes after interceptive FPM extraction depend on growth, eruption and occlusion together, which is why the guideline expects shared input from a paediatric or general dentist and a specialist orthodontist.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A two-perspective decision

FPM treatment-planning decisions should ideally be made following input from both the general dental practitioner or paediatric dentist and a specialist orthodontist [1]. Elective extraction of a compromised FPM with uncertain long-term prognosis must always be considered within the context of the patient and their underlying occlusion [2].

## Why combined services are the gold standard

Referral to centres where combined orthodontic and paediatric services are available is encouraged to allow comprehensive treatment planning and is considered the gold standard [3]. Where this is not possible, the guideline supports the attending clinician, but the implication for a starting GDP is clear: when a child has one or more questionable FPMs that are not in the acute pain category, the proper move is to stabilise, refer or seek combined input rather than to extract on the basis of one perspective alone.

citations.quote: FPM treatment-planning decisions should ideally be made following input from both the general dental practitioner (GDP) or paediatric dentist and a specialist orthodontist.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Introduction

citations.quote: the elective extraction of compromised FPMs with an uncertain long-term prognosis should always be considered within the context of the patient and their underlying occlusion;
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), Introduction

citations.quote: Referral to centres where combined orthodontic and paediatric services are available is encouraged to allow comprehensive treatment planning to be undertaken and should be considered the gold standard.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), General principles and practical guidance

firstPrinciples.title: A panoramic radiograph is mandatory before FPM extraction planning
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Without a recent DPT showing the full developing dentition, the radiographic predictors that drive timing and TPM-dependent decisions cannot be assessed.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the assessment requires

A full dental assessment must include a radiographic screen with a Dental Panoramic Tomograph to check the presence, position and normal formation of the full developing permanent dentition [1]. The interceptive timing guidance does not apply if access to a recent DPT to assess SPM development and position, and the presence or absence of TPMs, is not available [2].

## Why this is non-negotiable

The predictors used to time extraction (early bifurcation mineralisation of the SPM, SPM angulation, TPM presence) all live on the panoramic radiograph. Without it, the clinician cannot tell whether a child sits inside the favourable 8 to 10 year SPM-developing window or outside it, and cannot tell whether the affected quadrant will end up with two molar units or one. A GDP confronted with a child with compromised FPMs but no recent DPT should obtain one before any irreversible decision.

citations.quote: A full dental assessment must include a radiographic screen with a Dental Panoramic Tomograph (DPT) to check for the presence, position and normal formation of the full developing permanent dentition.
citations.source: RCS A Guideline for the Extraction of First Permanent Molars in Children (2023), General principles and practical guidance

subjects.title: Palatally ectopic maxillary canine
subjects.description: RCS Faculty of Dental Surgery (2022) guidance on diagnosing and managing palatally ectopic maxillary canines: when to suspect, how to localise, and how to choose between watch, intercept, expose-and-align, remove, or transplant.

workflows.title: Diagnosis and localisation of a palatally ectopic maxillary canine
workflows.overview:
## 1. Screen by palpation from age 8

Clinical inspection and **buccal palpation** of the alveolus in the canine region is recommended **annually from age 8**. The eruption rule of thumb is that a normally erupting canine should be **palpable in the buccal sulcus by 10 to 11 years**.

### Suspect ectopia if
- The canine is **not palpable** in the buccal sulcus by **10 to 11 years**
- Palpation reveals an **asymmetrical eruption pattern**
- The position of adjacent teeth implies a malposition of the permanent canine
- There is **abnormal mobility** of the adjacent permanent teeth

### Late-eruption thresholds
- Girls: maxillary canine erupting after **12.3 years**
- Boys: maxillary canine erupting after **13.1 years**

## 2. Comprehensive assessment

A suspected ectopic canine triggers a full malocclusion assessment, including accurate localisation of the canine. Look for the genetic-cluster anomalies that travel with palatal ectopia:
- Missing, malformed or **diminutive lateral incisors**
- **Absence of crowding**
- **Late-developing dentitions**
- Family history of palatal canines
- Previous impaction of an upper first permanent molar (raises both palatal canine impaction and incisor root resorption risk)

## 3. Decide if radiographs are appropriate

- Radiographs **before 10 to 11 years are usually of little benefit**
- Past that age, with clinical suspicion, take films to localise the canine and screen for resorption

## 4. Localise using parallax

**Parallax** is the apparent displacement of an object when the observer moves. In radiography, two films are taken with the **x-ray tube head in two different positions**.

### Horizontal parallax (preferred)
- **Upper standard occlusal** (midline view) **+ periapical** centred on the canine region, OR
- **Two periapicals**: one on the upper central incisor, one on the canine region
- More reliable than vertical parallax for localising unerupted canines

### Vertical parallax
- **Upper standard occlusal** (midline, beam aimed downwards) **+ panoramic** (beam aimed upwards at about 8 degrees), OR
- **Periapical** (bisected angle, beam downwards) **+ panoramic** (beam upwards at about 8 degrees)
- Less reliable; reliability may improve by increasing tube-head angulation

### Reading parallax
- Object that **moves with the tube** = **palatal**
- Object that **moves against the tube** = **buccal** (SLOB rule)

## 5. Consider CBCT only when conventional films are insufficient

- Small field-of-view CBCT can localise the canine and detect incisor root resorption
- Higher effective dose than conventional radiography
- **No indication for routine CBCT** (British Orthodontic Society guidance)
- SEDENTEXCT and UK guidance: small FOV CBCT **only when conventional radiographs fail to provide adequate information** to construct a treatment plan
- If unsure, seek the opinion of a **specialist in dental and maxillofacial radiology** before requesting CBCT

## 6. Document and refer

- Record the canine position, contact relationship of lateral incisor and first premolar, and any signs of incisor root resorption
- Treatment planning is not straightforward owing to the number of patient and orthodontic factors involved; the RCS strongly recommends that practitioners **seek the opinion of a specialist** before initiating any treatment option

workflows.title: Treatment decision for a palatally ectopic maxillary canine
workflows.overview:
## 1. Confirm position before any treatment

Radiographic examination should be carried out initially to confirm the position of the unerupted canine. Patient and parent counselling on the various treatment options is **essential** to ensure fully informed consent.

Five options sit on the table: interceptive extraction of the primary canine, surgical exposure and orthodontic alignment, surgical removal of the ectopic canine, autotransplantation, and no active treatment with observation.

## 2. Option 1: interceptive extraction of the primary canine [SIGN Grade A]

In carefully selected cases where the ectopic permanent canine is **not severely displaced**, extracting the adjacent primary canine can improve the position of the ectopic permanent canine.

### Patient selection
- Age **approximately 10 to 13 years**
- **Better results in the absence of crowding**
- The permanent canine is **not severely displaced**

### Caveats
- The need to **maintain space**, or even **create additional space**, requires consideration
- If radiographic examination shows **no improvement at 12 months** post-extraction, move to alternative treatment
- Original studies reported success around **78%**, later confirmed at around **62%**, but systematic reviews have not found sufficiently robust evidence to support **routine** extraction; counsel the patient that surgical exposure and orthodontic alignment may still be required

## 3. Option 2: surgical exposure and orthodontic alignment [SIGN Grade C]

Indicated when the case is not suitable for interceptive extraction. Patient selection drives prognosis.

### Patient must be
- Willing to wear **fixed orthodontic appliances**
- Well motivated, with **good dental health** (treatment time is often prolonged)

### Canine position must allow alignment
- The degree of malposition should not be so great that orthodontic alignment is impractical, e.g. **close proximity to the midline**, **above the apices of adjacent teeth**, or **horizontal angulation**

### Age and prognosis
- Optimal time is **adolescence**
- Likelihood of success **decreases with age in adults**, with increased risk of **ankylosis** and replacement resorption of the canine crown; treatment time is also longer
- **Open vs closed exposure**: no clear evidence one is superior for final position, pain, aesthetics, periodontal health, length of treatment or cost; **repeat surgery is more common with closed exposure**

## 4. Option 3: surgical removal of the palatally ectopic canine [SIGN Grade C]

Considered when active alignment is declined or impractical, or when the ectopic canine is causing harm.

### Indications
- Patient declines active treatment and/or is happy with their dental appearance
- **Radiographic evidence of early root resorption of an adjacent incisor** (but if root resorption is severe enough to require extraction of the incisor, exposure and alignment of the canine is usually indicated instead)
- Severe malposition where alignment and transplantation are not being considered
- Pathological change, or retention would impede orthodontic tooth movement

### Aesthetic prerequisites
- Best results when there is **good contact between the lateral incisor and first premolar**, or the patient is willing to undergo orthodontic treatment to **substitute the first premolar for the canine**
- Premolar can be cosmetically reshaped: **mesiopalatal rotation**, **buccal root torque**, and/or **grinding the palatal cusp**

### Risks to discuss
- Possible **damage to roots or neurovascular supply of adjacent teeth** during surgical removal
- If a prosthetic replacement may follow (canine removal and/or loss of a severely resorbed incisor), get a **restorative opinion at the outset**, especially if implants are likely

## 5. Option 4: autotransplantation [SIGN Grade B]

Not a first choice. Considered when other active or interceptive options have failed or are inappropriate, or for grossly displaced canines, or when prolonged orthodontic treatment is unacceptable.

### Prerequisites
- **Adequate space** for the canine
- **Sufficient alveolar bone** to accept the transplanted tooth
- **Good prognosis** for the canine, with **no evidence of ankylosis**
- Best results when the canine is removed with **minimal trauma** and **before closure of the apex**

### Postoperative
- Stabilise the transplanted tooth with a **sectional archwire for six weeks**
- If more than **three-quarters of the root is formed**, root canal therapy should be commenced **within ten days** of transplantation
- Long-term (>5-year) prognosis of transplanted palatally ectopic canines is not yet evaluated; for other transplanted teeth, success can be as high as **90%**

## 6. Option 5: no active treatment, leave and observe [SIGN Grade C]

### Acceptable when
- The patient does not want treatment or is happy with their dental appearance
- **No evidence of root resorption** of adjacent teeth or other pathology
- Ideally, **good contact between lateral incisor and first premolar**, or the primary canine has a **good prognosis**
- Severely displaced canines remote from the dentition with no pathology may be left in situ

### Ongoing duties
- Regular **clinical examination** to ensure the unerupted canine is not becoming a risk to the patient's wellbeing
- No firm guidance exists on how often to take radiographs in the absence of clinical signs or symptoms

## 7. Decision summary for the GDP

1. **Suspect early** (palpate from age 8, alarm at 10 to 11)
2. **Localise with parallax** and screen for incisor resorption
3. **Refer for specialist opinion** before any active treatment
4. **In a selected 10 to 13 year old without crowding and mild displacement**: discuss interceptive primary canine extraction, with the caveat that exposure and alignment may still be needed
5. **In an adolescent with a co-operative patient and a canine that can be aligned**: surgical exposure with orthodontic alignment
6. **If incisor resorption is occurring early or canine is severely malposed**: surgical removal (or rarely transplantation)
7. **If the patient is older, asymptomatic, with good lateral-to-premolar contact**: leave and observe with clinical follow-up

firstPrinciples.title: Maxillary canine impaction is common, mostly palatal, and a problem GDPs will see
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: How often a tooth gets stuck dictates how prepared a general dentist needs to be. The maxillary canine sits near the top of that list, behind only the lower wisdom tooth.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A 1.5% problem, second only to lower 8s

The maxillary canine is second only to the mandibular third molar in frequency of impaction, with a prevalence of about **1.5%** [1]. That is high enough that any GDP doing routine paediatric and adolescent care will encounter it.

## Palatal is the common pattern

Numerous sources in the literature suggest that ectopic canines occur **palatally with a much greater frequency than they do buccally** [2]. Buccal canines have not been studied as extensively, partly because a greater proportion of buccal canines erupt naturally without active intervention. The clinical consequence is that GDPs should mentally default to palpating the buccal sulcus to **rule out** ectopia, and assume the canine is palatal until proven otherwise when it is missing from the buccal sulcus at age 10 to 11.

## The cost of missing it

Failure to diagnose and manage an ectopic upper canine efficiently can result in more complex remedial treatment becoming necessary, costly in clinical time for both practitioner and patient, and there is also the risk of damage to adjacent teeth, which may lead to litigation claims [3].

firstPrinciples.title: Palatal ectopia is a polygenic anomaly that travels with other dental signs
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Palatal canine impaction does not appear in isolation. It clusters with specific incisor and developmental anomalies, which is why a GDP can predict it from features visible elsewhere in the mouth.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Polygenic, with familial clustering

The aetiology of ectopic palatal canines remains unclear, but is **likely to be polygenic**. This is supported by evidence that palatally ectopic canines occur more frequently than expected among family members [1].

## The signature dental cluster

There is a significant association with other dental anomalies that are often considered to have a genetic origin, such as **missing, malformed or diminutive lateral incisors**, an **absence of crowding**, and **late-developing dentitions** [2]. A child whose lateral incisors are peg-shaped or absent, who has well-spaced arches rather than crowded ones, and whose teeth have erupted late, sits in a higher prior probability for palatal canine ectopia.

## What this changes in clinic

When a GDP spots one of those features in a 7 to 9 year old, that is the trigger to make a habit of buccal canine palpation from age 8, ask about family history, and pay closer attention as the child approaches the 10 to 11 year palpation milestone. The clinical move is **anticipation**, not surprise.

citations.source: RCS Palatally Ectopic Maxillary Canine (2022), Introduction

firstPrinciples.title: A normally erupting canine is buccally palpable by age 10 to 11
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Putting a finger on the buccal sulcus is the cheapest, fastest screening test in dentistry. Knowing the age threshold turns it into a real test rather than a habit.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The 10 to 11 year palpation milestone

The majority of canines undergoing normal eruption should be **palpable in the buccal sulcus by 10 to 11 years of age** [1]. A canine that is not palpable buccally by then is the cardinal sign that should prompt the GDP to consider ectopia, alongside an asymmetrical eruption pattern, the position of adjacent teeth implying a malposition, or abnormal mobility of the adjacent permanent teeth [2].

## Late eruption thresholds

Maxillary canines erupting after approximately **12.3 years in girls and 13.1 years in boys** may be considered late [3]. These ages are not when to start worrying, they are when to be sure something is wrong if the canine has not appeared.

## Where the screening starts

Clinical inspection and buccal palpation of the alveolus in the canine region are recommended **annually from age 8** [4]. Two years of negative palpation builds the baseline that lets the practitioner notice when the canine fails to appear on schedule.

firstPrinciples.title: Incisor root resorption is the main hazard, and it has a narrow age window
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The reason ectopic canines are not just an aesthetic problem is that they damage neighbours. The risk window is age-bounded, which changes how urgently a young patient is referred.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Resorption is the headline risk

The main risk from ectopic canines is **root resorption of adjacent teeth, usually the incisors** [1]. One CBCT study detected resorption in **66.7% of permanent lateral incisors** adjacent to ectopic maxillary canines, although not always of clinical significance [2].

## A narrow age window

Root resorption of incisors by palatally ectopic canines **rarely starts after 14 years of age** and occurs **most frequently between 11 and 12 years** [3]. That timing maps neatly onto the age at which the GDP should already be suspicious from failed palpation. The window where damage is happening is the same window where good screening would catch it.

## What this changes for the GDP

An 11 to 12 year old with a non-palpable canine is not someone to leave for another year. The risk of harm to adjacent incisors is at its peak. Localisation films and a specialist referral belong in that visit, not in the next recall.

firstPrinciples.title: Other sequelae are real but less frequent than incisor resorption
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Beyond the incisors, two other things can go wrong with an unerupted ectopic canine. Their lower frequency does not let the GDP forget about them, especially in adults who present late.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Crown resorption of the canine itself

Resorption of the canine crown is a recognised sequela that is **most likely to occur in adults**, with quoted frequencies of **up to 14%** [1]. This is one reason a long-retained, unerupted ectopic canine in an adult is worth reviewing rather than assuming it is dormant forever.

## Cystic change

Cystic changes can also develop around an unerupted canine, although the frequency of this is **generally thought to be low** [2]. Combined with the crown-resorption point above, the take-home for a GDP following an adult with a leave-and-observe canine is that periodic clinical review remains worthwhile, even when the patient is asymptomatic.

## Why this matters when leaving canines alone

The RCS option of "no active treatment, leave and observe" is conditional on no current pathology. The duty of regular clinical examination exists precisely because crown resorption and cystic change can develop later. No firm guidance currently exists as to how frequently radiographic checks should be carried out in the absence of relevant clinical signs or symptoms [3].

firstPrinciples.title: Horizontal parallax is more reliable than vertical for localisation
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Two films and a tube-head shift are enough to localise most ectopic canines. Knowing which shift to choose is what separates a confident referral from a guess.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What parallax actually is

Parallax is the apparent displacement of an object because of different positions of the observer. In radiography, two films are taken with the **x-ray tube head in two different positions**, and the shift can be in the **horizontal plane** (horizontal parallax) or **vertical plane** (vertical parallax) [1].

## Horizontal beats vertical

Research has shown that the **horizontal parallax technique is more reliable than vertical parallax in localising unerupted canines** [2]. The reliability of vertical parallax might be improved by increasing tube-head angulation, but the default choice when the GDP has the option should be horizontal.

## Practical pairings

For horizontal parallax, the standard pairings are an **upper standard occlusal plus a periapical centred on the canine region**, or two periapicals (one on the upper central incisor, one on the canine region) [3]. Reading the films uses the SLOB rule: an object that moves with the tube head is palatal, an object that moves against the tube head is buccal. Given that palatal ectopia is the dominant pattern, the parallax test is mostly used to confirm the suspected diagnosis and locate the cusp tip relative to neighbouring roots.

firstPrinciples.title: CBCT is reserved, not routine, for ectopic canine imaging
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: More information always sounds better, but radiation dose is a real cost. The current rule is to earn the CBCT by exhausting plain films first.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What CBCT can add

Small field-of-view (FOV) CBCT can be used for the **localisation of ectopic canines** and the **identification of root resorption in incisor teeth** [1]. Three-dimensional information settles questions that overlapping 2D images cannot, particularly the precise spatial relationship between the canine and the lateral incisor root.

## Why it is not the default

CBCT is typically associated with a **higher overall effective dose of ionising radiation than conventional radiography** [2]. UK and European guidance, including SEDENTEXCT, restricts small FOV CBCT to **selected cases where conventional radiographs fail to provide adequate information** to construct a treatment plan [3]. The British Orthodontic Society orthodontic radiographs guidelines state explicitly that **there is no indication for the routine use of CBCT** [4].

## How a GDP handles this

Get the parallax pair first. If those films answer the position and resorption questions, the case is staged with no further imaging. If they do not, and uncertainty persists about whether CBCT is justified, the appropriate action is to seek the opinion of a specialist in dental and maxillofacial radiology before requesting it.

firstPrinciples.title: Interceptive primary canine extraction works in selected cases, but the evidence is not conclusive
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Removing the deciduous canine is the simplest possible intervention. Its place in the workflow depends on understanding both its real success rate and its evidence ceiling.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The original promise and the later checks

In carefully selected cases where the ectopic permanent canine is not severely displaced, there is some evidence that **interceptive extraction of the adjacent primary canine can result in an improvement in the position of an ectopic permanent canine** [1]. The original Ericson and Kurol study found that **78% of palatally ectopic canines reverted to a normal path of eruption** following extraction of the primary canine, although success appeared to reduce as the degree of malposition increased. A later investigation confirmed the finding with a slightly lower success rate of **62%** [2].

## What systematic reviews say

Despite the encouraging case-series data, **systematic reviews have failed to find sufficiently robust scientific evidence to support the routine extraction of the primary maxillary canine** to facilitate eruption of an ectopic permanent successor [3]. Further well-reported randomised controlled trials are required.

## How a GDP frames the conversation

The RCS position is that it is reasonable to consider interceptive extraction in carefully selected cases (age 10 to 13, mild displacement, ideally absence of crowding), provided the patient and parent understand that **surgical exposure and orthodontic treatment may ultimately be required** and that the supporting evidence is not conclusive [4]. A 12-month radiographic review point is built in: if the canine has not improved by then, the plan moves to alternative treatment.

firstPrinciples.title: Surgical exposure and alignment is most successful in adolescence and worsens with age
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Time matters for the canine that needs to be brought down. The same operation that succeeds reliably in a teenager carries a poorer prognosis in an adult.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Adolescence is the optimal window

Many years of clinical experience have shown that surgical exposure and orthodontic alignment of a palatally ectopic canine **can be a highly successful treatment approach** [1]. Several sources concur that the **optimal time for surgical exposure and orthodontic alignment is during adolescence**.

## Adults: poorer prognosis, longer treatment

A study comparing palatally ectopic maxillary canine treatment in adolescents and adults concluded that the **prognosis for successful orthodontic resolution of an impacted canine in an adult is lower than in a younger patient** and that the prognosis worsens with age, because of the **increased risk of ankylosis and/or replacement resorption of the permanent canine crown**. When such treatment is undertaken, its successful completion should be expected to take considerably longer [2].

## Open vs closed exposure: equivalent except for repeat surgery

When comparing open with closed exposure techniques, there is currently **no clear evidence to support one surgical technique over the other** in terms of final tooth position, pain, discomfort, aesthetics, periodontal health, length of treatment or cost; the one consistent finding is that **repeat surgery is more common with the closed exposure technique** [3]. For a GDP referring a young patient, the timing argument is the strongest single factor in favour of acting in adolescence rather than waiting.

Furthermore, when such treatment is undertaken, its successful completion should be expected to take considerably longer.

firstPrinciples.title: Autotransplantation has tight prerequisites and a defined endodontic timer
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Transplanting a canine is rare, but when it is on the table the success conditions are specific and the post-operative timing is unforgiving.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Selection conditions

Transplantation is not normally considered unless other active or interceptive treatment has failed or is inappropriate. It can be considered if the patient is unwilling to wear orthodontic appliances, or the malposition is too great for orthodontic alignment to be practical [1]. The hard prerequisites are **adequate space available for the canine** and **sufficient alveolar bone to accept the transplanted tooth**, with **good prognosis for the canine and no evidence of ankylosis**, and best results when the canine can be **removed with minimal trauma and before closure of the apex** [2].

## The endodontic timer

Depending on the stage of root formation, specifically when **more than three-quarters of the root is formed**, the transplanted canine may require **root canal therapy to be commenced within ten days following transplantation** [3]. This is a hard rule of post-operative care, not an option.

## Outcome data

Early studies revealed disappointing long-term results, with high frequencies of root resorption. More recent studies using a **meticulous atraumatic surgical technique and stabilisation with a sectional archwire for six weeks** have reported better results, but the **long-term (longer than five years) prognosis of transplanted palatally ectopic canines has yet to be evaluated**, although for other transplanted teeth success can be **as high as 90%** [4]. For a GDP, the practical relevance is that this is a defined specialist option with specific technique demands, not a routine fall-back.

citations.quote: Transplantation is not normally considered unless other possible active (or interceptive) treatment has failed or is considered to be inappropriate. This treatment option can be considered if the patient is unwilling to wear orthodontic appliances, or the degree of malposition is too great for orthodontic alignment to be practical.
citations.source: RCS Palatally Ectopic Maxillary Canine (2022), Treatment, Section 4

The prognosis should be good for the canine tooth to be transplanted with no evidence of ankylosis. The best results are achieved if the ectopic canine can be removed with minimal trauma and before closure of the apex.

workflows.title: Diagnosis and assessment of an unerupted maxillary incisor
workflows.overview:
## 1. Recognise the clinical presentation

Failure of eruption associated with maxillary permanent incisors usually presents in the **mixed dentition stage** and is **most often noticed between 7 and 9 years of age**. Early diagnosis matters because of aesthetic and psychosocial impact on the child.

Delayed eruption can be considered when **any one** of the following is true:
- The contralateral incisor erupted **more than 6 months earlier**
- The maxillary incisors remain unerupted **more than one year after the lower incisors erupt**
- There is significant deviation from the normal eruption sequence (e.g. lateral incisor erupting before the central)

## 2. Take a focused history

### Local factors that delay eruption
- Early extraction or loss of primary teeth (with or without space loss)
- Prolonged retention of primary teeth
- Crowding in the upper labial segment
- Previous trauma to the primary dentition
- Localised pathology: supernumerary teeth, odontomes, rarely cysts

### Less frequent associations
- Cleft lip and palate
- Cleidocranial dysplasia and other syndromes with multiple supernumerary teeth

A history of **trauma to the primary dentition** should be sought and documented, with approximate dates and a description of the magnitude and direction of the impact.

## 3. Clinical examination

Intra-orally, look for and record:
- **Retained primary incisors** beyond their normal exfoliation date
- **Spacing, rotations and displacement** of permanent teeth in the upper incisor region
- **Drift of the lateral incisor** into the central incisor space (a clue to disturbed development)
- **Labial or palatal swellings** that may indicate the site of an unerupted incisor
- Angulation and inclination of adjacent teeth
- Available space for eruption: roughly **9 mm for a permanent maxillary central** and **7 mm for a permanent maxillary lateral**

## 4. Radiographic examination

Intra-oral radiographs are the first line.

### First-line films
- **Periapical** views of the upper incisor region, and / or
- **Upper standard occlusal**

These identify the unerupted tooth, any supernumeraries or odontomes, and underlying pathology. They also enable **horizontal or vertical parallax** to localise the bucco-lingual position of the unerupted incisor.

### Adjuncts
- A **cephalometric** radiograph helps with very high impactions and assesses bucco-lingual inclination of the crown and root
- **CBCT** in selected cases gives a three-dimensional view of the impacted tooth and surrounding structures

### When to use CBCT
- Only when the required information **cannot be adequately obtained using lower-dose conventional radiography** (SEDENTEXCT, 2012)
- Particularly useful when **dilaceration is suspected**, because the degree of crown-root angulation can be assessed and the optimal direction of orthodontic traction planned

## 5. Decide who needs referral

The RCS recommends that examination and treatment planning **ideally happen in a multi-disciplinary clinic**, with paediatric dental and / or oral surgery colleagues. A starting GDP should refer when:
- A supernumerary, odontome, or other obstruction is identified
- Suspected dilaceration of the permanent incisor
- High vertical position of the impacted incisor
- Any uncertainty about diagnosis or surgical planning

workflows.title: Management decision for an unerupted maxillary incisor
workflows.overview:
## 1. Rest the plan on two pillars

Irrespective of cause, the **general principles** of management are:
1. Provide **adequate space** in the dental arch for the unerupted incisor
2. **Remove any obstruction** to eruption (supernumerary, odontome, retained primary tooth)

Further eruption can then be promoted by **surgical exposure**, with or without orthodontic traction, depending on patient and dental factors.

## 2. Weigh the patient factors

- **Medical history** — any condition that affects orthodontic or surgical care
- **Age** — most cases present at 7 to 9 years; spontaneous eruption after supernumerary removal is more likely if the supernumerary is removed at **8 to 9 years of age**
- **Compliance** — fixed-appliance traction is demanding; younger children may not tolerate it

## 3. Weigh the dental factors

- **Retained primary teeth** — extract them; if the permanent successor is close to eruption with no other obstruction, it may erupt spontaneously
- **Vertical position** of the impacted incisor — the **higher** the position, the **less likely** spontaneous eruption is. In one series, only ~28% of incisors initially at the apical-third level erupted spontaneously after supernumerary removal
- **Stage of root development** — evidence is mixed; some series suggest immature roots erupt more readily after obstruction removal, others find no difference
- **Nature of any obstruction**
  - Supernumerary morphology and degree of incisor displacement both affect outcome
  - **Tuberculate supernumeraries and odontomes** more often obstruct eruption than **conical** supernumeraries
  - About **one third of compound** and **one half of complex odontomes** prevent eruption of teeth
- **Unfavourable root formation (dilaceration)** — typically caused by trauma to the primary predecessor; takes longer to align and has a poorer prognosis

## 4. Discuss the risks of treatment

Explain to the patient and parent:
- Failure of eruption
- Ankylosis
- External root resorption
- Poor gingival aesthetics

In most cases treatment is successful, but these risks are real and shape the choice of approach.

## 5. Choose between management options

### A. Removal of the obstruction only (and monitor)
- After removal of a supernumerary, retrospective data suggests **49 to 91%** of permanent maxillary incisors erupt spontaneously
- Up to **9 to 12 months** is a reasonable wait in the **younger patient (<9 years)** with an immature incisor before further intervention
- Spontaneous eruption is more likely when **adequate space** is available; consider creating space with a removable or fixed appliance
- Time to erupt can be up to **18 months**

### B. Removal of obstruction with surgical exposure (open or closed)
- For the **older patient (>9 years)** with a mature incisor, or if the incisor is high, consider exposure and bonding of an attachment **at the same operation** as obstruction removal
- Avoids a second general anaesthetic
- Success of exposure with traction has been reported to **exceed 90%**
- **Open exposure**: simple elliptical excision over the crown; useful for very superficial soft-tissue impactions; an apically repositioned flap can be used when the incisor is higher, but this risks longer crowns and poor soft-tissue aesthetics
- **Closed exposure**: a mucoperiosteal flap is raised, an attachment with gold chain or traction ligature is bonded (ideally palatal), and the flap is replaced. Early studies suggest superior periodontal and pulpal outcomes versus open exposure; longitudinal data shows shorter clinical crowns and better bone support

### C. Incisor removal
Indicated when the incisor cannot be aligned (significant **dilaceration** or **ankylosis with infra-occlusion**). Then choose:
- **Maintain space** for prosthetic replacement (initially fixed or removable, eventually implant once growth is complete)
- **Move the lateral incisor** into the central position for camouflage
- **Accept spontaneous space closure**, then re-open space with a fixed appliance for definitive restoration

Prolonged absence of a tooth leads to alveolar bone loss in height and width, which can complicate later implant placement.

### D. Manage an ankylosed incisor
For an ankylosed permanent maxillary incisor:
- **Periodic follow-up** with composite build-up for minor infra-occlusion
- **Repositioning** (surgical dislodgement, osteotomy, or distraction osteogenesis)
- **Extraction with orthodontic space closure**
- **Decoronation** while growth is still active, to preserve alveolar height and width
- **Extraction and prosthetic replacement** if growth is nearing completion

There is **insufficient high-level evidence** to compare these options directly.

### E. Autotransplantation
- Most commonly the **lower second premolar** is transplanted into the maxillary central incisor site
- Advantage: a vital tooth with preserved periodontium, allowing morphological reshaping coronally
- Disadvantages: poor donor morphology may need extensive restorative work, occlusal interference from a palatal cusp, and risk of rapid external root resorption with premature loss

## 6. Plan monitoring

- After obstruction removal alone, review at intervals; allow up to **9 to 12 months** in younger children before re-intervening
- Patients with impacted maxillary central incisors have an **increased risk of further developmental disturbance**, including **ipsilateral maxillary canine displacement**; build a longer surveillance window into the orthodontic plan
- Prefer a multi-disciplinary clinic for joint decisions on timing, surgical choice and attachment position

firstPrinciples.title: An unerupted maxillary incisor is one of the few orthodontic problems that announces itself in primary school
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Most ectopic teeth are caught later by a dentist who notices something missing. The maxillary incisor sits at the front of the mouth and at the front of childhood social development.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A mixed-dentition presentation

Failure of eruption of a permanent maxillary incisor usually presents in the mixed dentition and is most often noticed between the ages of 7 and 9 [1]. Before that age the contralateral side has not yet given a comparison; much later than that and the cosmetic and developmental consequences of leaving the gap have set in.

## Why this matters

Missing and unerupted maxillary incisors can be regarded as unattractive and have a potentially negative impact on facial and dental aesthetics, with knock-on effects on self-esteem and social interaction [2]. The visible front gap is what brings the parent through the door, but the hidden cost is psychosocial.

## The clinical move

A GDP screening a 7 to 9 year old should compare upper to lower and left to right, and should consider eruption to be delayed if the contralateral incisor erupted more than 6 months earlier, if the upper incisors are still unerupted more than a year after the lowers, or if the eruption sequence is out of order [3]. Any of these earns a focused history and films.

firstPrinciples.title: Physical obstruction by a supernumerary or odontome is the dominant cause of unerupted maxillary incisors
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Many things can delay an upper incisor, but one cause sits well above all the others. Knowing the hierarchy tells the GDP what to look for first on the radiograph.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A short cause list with a clear leader

The most common causes of failure of eruption of the permanent maxillary incisor are physical obstruction due to a supernumerary tooth or odontome, and trauma to the primary dentition that contributes to dilaceration of the permanent successor [1]. Of these, by far the most frequent cause is the presence of a supernumerary tooth [2].

## Where supernumeraries cluster

The anterior maxilla is a common site for the development of supernumerary teeth or odontomes [3]. Around 90 to 98% of maxillary supernumerary teeth develop within the midline and maxillary central incisor region [4]. The radiograph that confirms an unerupted central incisor must always be read with that hot zone in mind.

## What this changes in clinic

When a 7 to 9 year old presents with a non-erupting upper central incisor, the GDP should expect to find a supernumerary or odontome on the periapical or upper standard occlusal film. The history about earlier trauma is the second question, not the first.

firstPrinciples.title: Trauma to a primary incisor can dilacerate the permanent successor
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: An injury that looks trivial at age three can produce a tooth that fails to erupt at age eight. The mechanism explains why a careful trauma history matters in this presentation.
firstPrinciples.body:
## How the mechanism works

Dilaceration is defined as an acute deviation of the long axis of the tooth, located in the crown or the root, originating from a traumatic non-axial displacement of already formed hard tissue in relation to the developing soft tissue [1]. The permanent maxillary incisor is the classical victim because of its position immediately above and behind the apex of the primary central incisor.

## Why this is a common pathway

Traumatic injuries to the primary dentition are relatively common, with a prevalence reported in the range of 11 to 30% [2]. A proportion of these injuries displace the developing permanent crown relative to its root, and the resulting dilaceration can prevent normal eruption.

## Clinical implications

A dilacerated incisor takes longer to align and has a poorer prognosis for successful eruption than an incisor impacted by simple physical obstruction [3]. When dilaceration is suspected, CBCT is the imaging modality of choice because the optimal direction of orthodontic traction depends on knowing the crown-root angulation in three dimensions [4]. None of this is possible without first asking the parent about earlier knocks to the upper baby teeth.

firstPrinciples.title: The vertical position of the impacted incisor is the strongest predictor of spontaneous eruption
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: When a child arrives with an unerupted upper central, the question is whether removing the obstruction is going to be enough. The radiographic position of the crown answers most of that question.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Position dictates the odds

The vertical position of the impacted permanent maxillary incisor has been shown to influence both successful spontaneous eruption and the time taken to erupt [1]. The higher the vertical position of an unerupted maxillary incisor, the less likely it is to erupt spontaneously after an obstructing supernumerary tooth is removed [2].

## A specific anchor figure

In one retrospective study, only 28.6% of unilaterally impacted permanent maxillary incisors erupted spontaneously when their initial position was at the level of the apical third of the contralateral erupted incisor [3]. That number sets a working threshold for the GDP: a high impaction is unlikely to come down on its own.

## How this drives treatment planning

A low impaction, an immature root, and adequate arch space tilt the plan toward removal of the obstruction and waiting up to 9 to 12 months for spontaneous eruption. A high impaction tilts the plan toward simultaneous surgical exposure and bonding of an attachment at the time of obstruction removal, on the grounds that a second general anaesthetic is something to be avoided when it can be predicted.

firstPrinciples.title: Most incisors blocked by a supernumerary will erupt once the obstruction is removed
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The conservative pathway often works. Knowing roughly how often it works lets a clinician plan the watchful-waiting period with confidence.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The retrospective range

Following the removal of a supernumerary tooth, retrospective evaluation suggests that between 49 and 91% of permanent maxillary incisors will erupt spontaneously [1]. The reported time to erupt varies and can be up to 18 months [2].

## Adequate space tilts the odds further

Spontaneous eruption is more likely if space exists in the dental arch to accommodate the unerupted incisor [3]. A prospective study combining maxillary expansion with obstruction removal reported 82% spontaneous eruption [4]. Space creation, with a removable appliance or a sectional or full-arch fixed appliance, is therefore part of the conservative plan rather than a separate option.

## What this means in clinic

For a younger child (under 9) with an immature incisor and an adequate arch, removing the supernumerary, creating or preserving space, and waiting up to 9 to 12 months is reasonable. Beyond that window, around 30 to 54% of impacted incisors will still need further surgical intervention to bring them in [5], so the threshold for re-assessment must be agreed up front.

firstPrinciples.title: Closed eruption gives better long-term periodontal outcomes than open exposure
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Surgical exposure of an unerupted incisor has two recognised techniques. The choice has long-term consequences for crown length and bone support, not just short-term ones for alignment.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Two techniques, one tooth

In open exposure, the soft tissue overlying the crown is excised; in closed eruption, a mucoperiosteal flap is raised, an attachment with a gold chain or traction ligature is bonded to the tooth, and the flap is replaced into its original position [1]. The tooth then erupts under intact mucosa.

## What the comparative evidence shows

There are only a few studies that have specifically compared the two techniques [2]. Early studies demonstrated superior results for closed eruption in terms of gingival, periodontal and pulpal status [3]. Longitudinal assessment has reported longer clinical crowns and decreased bone support in association with open eruption, particularly when an apically repositioned flap is used [4].

## What this changes in planning

For a high impaction or a tooth that is not very superficially placed, closed exposure is the default. Bonding the attachment to the palatal surface lets the orthodontist apply traction in the most favourable direction and reduces the risk of fenestration of the attachment through the thin overlying alveolar mucosa as the tooth is aligned. Open exposure stays in the toolkit for the rare soft-tissue impaction with adequate attached gingiva.

firstPrinciples.title: Combining surgery in one operation matters because most patients are children under general anaesthesia
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: An eight-year-old who needs an obstruction removed today may need a second procedure later. The decision to combine the two changes the burden on the child and family.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The clinical reality

Most patients with unerupted maxillary incisors present in the mixed dentition stage and are children. Where surgical removal of the obstruction is needed, this is often performed under general anaesthesia. After supernumerary removal alone, between 30 and 54% of impacted permanent maxillary incisors require further surgical intervention to facilitate their eruption [1].

## The practice principle

It is good clinical practice to avoid the need for repeat general anaesthesia whenever possible, and so it is prudent to consider surgical exposure and bonding of an orthodontic attachment at the time of supernumerary removal [2]. The attachment can then be used later if required, to align the incisor and so avoid a second general anaesthetic.

## How this maps to age

In the younger patient (under 9 years) with an immature incisor, allowing 9 to 12 months for spontaneous eruption after obstruction removal is reasonable [3]. In the older patient (over 9 years) with a mature incisor, especially when the impaction is high, simultaneous exposure and bonding is the more sensible default [4].

firstPrinciples.title: An ankylosed incisor cannot be moved by orthodontic traction and changes the entire plan
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Ankylosis is one of the recognised risks of trying to bring an unerupted incisor into the arch. When it happens, the choice of next move depends on whether the child is still growing.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why ankylosis matters

Ankylosis is a potentially unfavourable complication of aligning unerupted permanent maxillary incisors [1]. An ankylosed tooth has lost its periodontal ligament and fused to bone, so orthodontic traction will not move it; it will sit infra-occluded as the surrounding alveolus continues to grow.

## Growth stage drives the decision

For an actively growing child, decoronation can be considered to preserve the width and vertical height of the alveolar bone for future restoration [2]. Where growth is nearing completion, extraction with replacement by a conventional or implant-supported prosthesis is the more usual route [3]. Other options include surgical repositioning (dislodgement, osteotomy, or distraction osteogenesis), extraction with orthodontic space closure, and periodic follow-up with composite build-up if the infra-occlusion is minor.

## A note on certainty

There is currently insufficient high-level evidence for comparing the effectiveness of different treatment methods relating to the ankylosed maxillary incisor [4]. The decision is therefore made case by case, with a multi-disciplinary team and explicit discussion of bone preservation, growth, and longer-term restorative options.

firstPrinciples.title: An impacted maxillary incisor predicts trouble for the canine on the same side
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The unerupted incisor is rarely the only developmental disturbance the child will face. Surveillance of the rest of the dentition is part of the long-term plan.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the data show

Patients with impacted permanent maxillary central incisors are reported to have an increased risk of further disruption to normal dental development. In a retrospective study, the prevalence of maxillary canine displacement on the same side as an unerupted incisor was significantly increased compared with the contralateral side [1].

## Why this changes follow-up

The ipsilateral canine is the next likely problem and the next likely radiographic find. A child who has had a supernumerary removed and a central incisor exposed and aligned still needs annual canine palpation from age 8, with a lower threshold for radiographic localisation if the canine is not palpable buccally by 10 to 11 years.

## A small extra burden, a large potential payoff

Adding a few minutes of canine palpation and a relevant film to a recall appointment is cheap. Catching a palatal canine early enough to attempt interceptive extraction of the primary canine, or to plan exposure and traction, is a much better outcome than discovering it late with associated incisor root resorption.
